data: Start with a quickstart, then use the groups below.
data.configure#Configure: Resource classes: Resource classes as Swarm services: default sizes and limits, how to add a class, replica counts, persistent classes, Rerun job with SSH, and the stack variable reference. Images: Run the runner in stock Linux and Windows images with a read-only mount, and bring your own image. Docker builds: Build container images from jobs with an opt-in service that mounts the host Docker engine, and compare the rootless and daemonless alternatives. MicroVM jobs: Run each job in its own microVM with Kata Containers on labeled Linux nodes, set up the nodes, and learn what the add-on costs and what it does not cover. Container mode: Run CircleCI Docker-executor jobs (docker - image and service containers) on Docker Swarm with no Kubernetes. A prototype agent, its architecture, security model, and limits.
data.contribute#Contribute: CI/CD: What the pipeline tests and when, the maintainer tasks and settings it needs, how the docs site is built, and how releases are signed and published. Releasing: How a merge to main becomes a signed GitHub release, how maintainers enable publishing, and how to recover from a failed release. Contributing: How to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request for machine runner swarm, a CircleCI Labs project.
data.get-started#Get started: Quickstart on Linux: Run a first job with CircleCI machine runner 3 on one Docker Swarm node in five steps. A trial: the node cannot join a cluster later. Quickstart on Windows Server: Run a first job on a Windows Server Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in five steps, using the stock Server Core image. Concepts: How Swarm services map to resource classes, what the token proxy does, what a clean environment covers, and how the default and hardened classes differ.
data.install#Install: Linux: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Ubuntu or RHEL, with one clean container for every job. Windows Server: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server 2022 or 2025, with one clean container for every job. Multi-node clusters: Join Linux, Windows, and Arm nodes to one Docker Swarm, place resource classes with labels and constraints, and open the ports that the nodes need.
data.more#More: Security: Threat model, token storage on Linux and Windows, the token proxy, hardening defaults, CircleCI-side controls, egress hosts, and BitLocker. FAQ: Short answers about the Swarm runner stack: what it is, support, comparisons with official runners, scaling, unsupported jobs, and node loss.
data.operate#Operate: Operations: Runbooks for status and logs, capacity, upgrades, token rotation, proxy restarts, and node drains, then reference for monitoring, backups, compatibility, and uninstall. Troubleshooting: Symptoms, causes and fixes for the Docker Swarm runner stack on Linux and Windows, with the error text to search for.
data.reference#Reference: Changelog: Release notes are on GitHub Releases. Read every release between yours and the one you install before you upgrade. Migrate from Docker Compose: Move from the old docker-compose.yml setup to the Docker Swarm stack, and map each Compose setting to its Swarm equivalent.

Images: Run the runner in stock Linux and Windows images with a read-only mount, and bring your own image. Docker builds: Build container images from jobs with an opt-in service that mounts the host Docker engine, and compare the rootless and daemonless alternatives. Container mode: Run CircleCI Docker-executor jobs (docker - image and service containers) on Docker Swarm with no Kubernetes. A prototype agent, its architecture, security model, and limits.

Container mode runs jobs that use the Docker executor, docker: [{image: ...}, {image: ...}], on the nodes of a Swarm, with no Kubernetes. With the machine classes of machine runner swarm, one Swarm serves both kinds of jobs.
Warning This is a prototype, and CircleCI does not support it. The unit tests and a Swarm test against a fake runner API and a fake init image pass. A run against the real CircleCI API is still to be done. Do not use it for production jobs yet. Refer to Status.
data.architecture#Architecture:
flowchart TB api["runner.circleci.comHTTPS 443, outbound only"] subgraph node["A worker node with the label container-mode=true"] direction TB agent["container-agentglobal Swarm servicethe only holder of the Docker socket"] sock["Docker engine of the node"] subgraph task["One job: containers, a network and a volume, all removed at the end"] direction LR pause["pauseholds the network namespace"] init["initcopies GOAT and the task agentinto the volume, then exits"] primary["primaryGOAT, then the task agent"] svc["service containersfor example a database"] end end agent -->|claims, reports| api agent -->|create, start, wait, remove| sock sock -.->|creates and removes| pause pause --- primary pause --- svc init -->|volume| primary primary -->|task agent: steps and output| apiThe agent is a global Swarm service. It starts on every worker with the label machine-runner-swarm.container-mode=true, and on no manager, no microVM node (machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true), no Docker-build node (machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true), and no node with the token proxy label (machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true). The token proxy keeps off container-mode nodes in turn.
The agent is the only container that mounts /var/run/docker.sock and its class tokens (Swarm secrets). It does not use the token proxy: whoever holds the socket, which is root-equivalent on its node, can read the secrets of the node, so a proxy would protect nothing.
Nothing is built or published. The service runs a stock Go image, pinned by digest, and compiles the Go sources in linux/stack/container-agent (Swarm configs named after their content) at start-up. A changed source updates the service, so docker stack deploy is the whole upgrade.
The code has two sides, so that the part that runs a job on an engine can later be offered upstream as a driver: the Docker driver (driver_docker.go, docker.go, behind the interface in driver.go) knows nothing of the runner API or class tokens, and the wrapper (main.go, wrapper.go, api.go: claim loop, slots, runner API) knows nothing of containers. A driver gets the task token of one task and no class token.
data.deploy#Deploy:
You need a Swarm set up as in the Linux quickstart, Docker Engine 24 or later, and a resource class and token for container mode. The nodes need access to Docker Hub and registry.k8s.io for the Go, init, and pause images.
Create the resource class and a token with the circleci CLI, and store the token in a secret. Do not reuse the token of a machine class.
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create docker-default-token - Label the workers that may run jobs. Never label a manager.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.container-mode=true worker-1 Edit MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_CLASSES in linux/stack/container-mode.yaml: replace CHANGE-ME with your namespace, and set the limits. Then deploy:
docker stack deploy -c linux/stack/runners.yaml -c linux/stack/container-mode.yaml runners Run a job. The example examples/container-mode.yml has a primary container and a PostgreSQL service on localhost:5432. Read the agent log with:
docker service logs runners_container-agent
data.limits#Limits: Limit Detail Prototype Not run against the real CircleCI API yet. Not supported by CircleCI (Status) Linux only Linux workers on amd64 and arm64 in principle. Only amd64 is tested (Windows) No Rerun job with SSH The agent publishes no port and passes no SSH settings to GOAT No Docker layer caching, no setup_remote_docker The job has no engine. Use the docker-build class from a machine class, or a daemonless builder No ECR authentication A job that uses aws_auth fails. Registry credentials with a user name and password work No service logs or lifecycle output in the CircleCI UI Read them on the node with docker logs while a job runs, or in the agent log No wait for service readiness Use dockerize -wait or a retry in the job, as with the Docker executor The job user A user: becomes the user of the Docker container. Container runner instead passes the name to GOAT, which needs a container that starts as root One limit pair for all services Container runner sets limits for each service image Orphans after a crash CircleCI keeps the job of a crashed agent until its own timeout The init image pin The pinned digest may give a task agent older than CircleCI expects. Watch for new tags, or unset MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_INIT_IMAGE
data.security-model#Security model:
The agent is a trusted component, like the Kubernetes service account of container runner.
Question Answer What holds the Docker socket? Only the agent, as root with a read-only root filesystem and no capabilities. The socket is root-equivalent on its node. linux/tests/container-mode.sh checks that no job container mounts it. The agent container also holds the Go compiler. For a smaller container, compile the sources into an image of your own (CGO_ENABLED=0 go build) and set image and entrypoint in the stack file Where are the class tokens? In Swarm secrets that only the agent mounts, and in its memory. No job container has a class token or a way to claim a job. The agent never runs on the node of the token proxy Where is the task token? In one environment variable of the primary container, which GOAT removes before the task agent starts. It is scoped to one job, but docker inspect on the node can read it, so the node must not hand the socket to jobs (Docker builds) Can one job reach another? Each job has its own bridge network, and Docker does not route between them. A job can reach the internet and the node through the gateway, as a machine class can What stops a runaway job? --cpus, --memory (without swap) and a process limit on every container, and a maximum run time What does a job container keep? Default capabilities without NET_RAW and MKNOD, no privileged mode, no devices, no host paths. It runs as the user of its image, or the user of the job Is it a virtual machine boundary? No. All containers of a node share its kernel. Use the machine runner orchestrator for untrusted code (Security) Which images does the agent trust? Those that the job names, as in the Docker executor Anyone who can change the job configuration of a project chooses the images that run on your nodes, as with any runner. Restrict who can use the class with the same controls as for a machine class.
data.settings#Settings:
Set these in the environment of the service in the stack file.
Variable Default Meaning MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_CLASSES none, required A JSON array of classes. Each entry has name (/), token_file (a Swarm secret: the bare token, or a runner config with an auth_token line), and the limits primary and service, each with cpus, memory_mb, and pids (default 4096) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_MAX_TASKS 2 Jobs at the same time on this node MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_MAX_RUN_TIME 5h The longest a job may run. After it, the agent reports a failure and removes the job MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_INIT_IMAGE circleci/runner-init: The init image. The stack file pins a digest MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_PAUSE_IMAGE registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 The image that holds the network namespace. The stack file pins a digest MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_PULL always always pulls a tag before each job. missing pulls only an image that the node lacks. An image pinned by digest is pulled once MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_RUNNER_API https://runner.circleci.com The runner API. Set the URL of your CircleCI server for a server installation MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_POLL_INTERVAL 3s The wait between claims when no job is queued MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_NAME the hostname The name that the agent gives CircleCI MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_DOCKER_SOCKET /var/run/docker.sock The Docker socket of the node, as seen inside the agent container MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_KEEP_FAILED unset true leaves the containers, network, and volume of a failed job for docker logs. The next start of the agent removes them. Only for debugging: a kept primary container holds the task token
data.sizing#Sizing:
Swarm sees only the agent service, so it cannot place jobs by free memory or CPU:
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CONTAINER_MAX_TASKS caps the jobs of a node. Choose it so that the cap times (the primary limit plus the service limits of a job) fits in the node. The default classes allow 4 GiB for the primary container and 2 GiB for each service, so a job with one service needs up to 6 GiB. A job with no free slot stays in the CircleCI queue and runs on another node. To scale out, label another worker. The agent needs up to 1 GiB while it compiles at start-up.
data.status#Status: Piece State Unit tests (linux/stack/container-agent, go test, run in CI) Pass: the container layout, limits, environment, GOAT settings, failure and retry paths, cleanup, the start-up sweep, the cap, and that no token reaches a log. The wrapper runs against a fake driver, and the Docker driver against a fake engine Swarm test (linux/tests/container-mode.sh, in Docker-in-Docker, with a fake runner API and a fake init image) Passes: no agent on a node with the proxy or microVM label, one job with a service on localhost, one failing job, the limits, no socket in the job, the cap, the cleanup, and the orphans Init image and GOAT The public circleci/runner-init image fills a volume in plain Docker, and its orchestrator run-task starts a task agent with the settings that the agent writes. Not part of the CI Real CircleCI job Not yet. A first run on a test class is the next step See also Concepts, Security, and FAQ: Can it run Docker executor jobs?.
data.the-life-of-a-job#The life of a job: The agent polls CircleCI with the token of each class, only while it has a free slot, because a claim assigns the job to it. The claim returns a task token, which fetches the job configuration. A job without a docker: list is a machine job, and the agent reports a failure. It pulls the init, pause and job images. Registry credentials from the job go to the engine for the pull and are never stored. Variables such as $DOCKERHUB_PASSWORD are expanded from the environment of the job. It creates a network and a volume, and starts the init container (no network), which copies orchestrator (GOAT) and circleci-agent into the volume at /opt/circleci/bin and exits. It starts the pause container, then each service container with the image, entrypoint, command, user and environment from the job, and the service limits of the class. All use --network container:, so a service listens on localhost for the primary container. It starts the primary container with the entrypoint /opt/circleci/bin/orchestrator run-task and the GOAT settings, including the task token, in one environment variable. GOAT starts the task agent with the token on its standard input and removes the settings from the environment before any step starts. The task agent reports steps and output to CircleCI itself. When the primary container stops, the agent removes the containers, network, and volume, and tells CircleCI that the job is cleaned up (after reporting a failure, if the primary container failed). If a container could not start, for example after a failed image pull, it returns the job to the queue, and reports a failure only when CircleCI has no retries left. On SIGTERM, the agent stops claiming and lets running jobs finish (stop_grace_period: 5h5m, as for the machine classes). At start-up it removes every container, network, and volume with its Docker label machine-runner-swarm.container-mode=1, the leftovers of a crash. Swarm updates the service stop-first, so two agents never run on one node.
data.what-it-is#What it is:
A job with a docker: list belongs to container runner, which starts one pod for each job. Container mode copies that design onto the Docker engine of a Swarm node:
Container runner on Kubernetes Container mode on Swarm The container agent, with Kubernetes RBAC to create pods The swarm container agent, with the Docker socket of its node One pod for each job One group of containers for each job: pause, init, primary, and one for each service Containers reach each other on localhost The same, through the network namespace of the pause container An init container copies the orchestrator (GOAT) and the task agent into an emptyDir The same init image copies them into a volume of the task A Kubernetes secret holds the task token The environment of the primary container holds it Pod resources limits --cpus and --memory on every container Kubernetes places pods on nodes with free resources A global agent on each opted-in node, and a cap on its jobs A class serves one mode. A class that a machine runner and a container agent both claim from sends jobs to the wrong one, and they fail at once. Use separate classes and tokens for each mode.
data.windows#Windows:
Windows is not supported. It needs:
A way to share one network namespace between containers, for the localhost behavior. Check whether the engine accepts --network container: for Windows containers. Windows images for the init step, GOAT, and the pause container, and the Windows build of the task agent. The named pipe \\.\pipe\docker_engine in place of the socket, an isolation mode with matching limits, Windows paths for the volume, and a different user model.

data: By default, jobs on these runners cannot reach a Docker engine, because access to a Docker daemon is root access to the machine. Docker builds are opt-in, one dedicated class at a time.
data.choose-a-pattern#Choose a pattern: Pattern Jobs get Root-equivalent on the node Status Platform A: host engine socket The full Docker API of the node Yes Built, with a stack file and an example Linux, and Windows images on Windows B: rootless BuildKit on the host Only a build API, through the socket of one BuildKit daemon No, but the daemon runs on the host Documented, not built Linux C: daemonless builder in the job Nothing from the host No Documented, not built Linux D: Docker daemon inside a microVM Its own daemon, in the VM of the job No, but the job has SYS_ADMIN inside a VM Built and tested with a fake API, in the microVM add-on Linux with KVM CircleCI lists Docker layer caching among the features that self-hosted runners do not support. Pattern A reuses the layer cache of the host engine, which every job on that node shares.
data.deploy-on-linux#Deploy on Linux:
Join a dedicated worker node (Multi-node clusters). Nothing is installed on it: runner-distributor installs the runner there.
Label the node:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true Create the resource class /linux-docker-build and the secret linux-docker-build-token (Resource classes).
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
docker stack deploy -c linux/stack/runners.yaml -c linux/stack/docker-build.yaml runners linux/stack/docker-build.yaml defines linux-docker-build. It mounts the socket and adds the job user to the group of the socket, so jobs need no sudo to run docker. The runner volume stays read-only, but a job that controls the engine can change runner-bin of its node, which only this class uses there. The cimg/base image includes the Docker CLI.
jobs: image: machine: true resource_class: /linux-docker-build steps: - checkout - run: docker build -t "app:${CIRCLE_SHA1:0:12}" . - run: name: Clean up, the engine outlives the job when: always command: docker image rm -f "app:${CIRCLE_SHA1:0:12}" || true The file examples/linux-docker-build.yml has the full job.
data.deploy-on-windows#Deploy on Windows:
windows\stack\docker-build.yaml defines windows-docker-build. It mounts the named pipe \\.\pipe\docker_engine and the host directory C:\Program Files\Docker read-only at C:\docker, which it appends to the PATH. Adjust the bind source if docker.exe lives elsewhere. It runs on a worker only, as on Linux, so it needs a Windows worker in the Swarm (Multi-node clusters). The single-node Swarm of the Windows quickstart has only a manager, and the class stays Pending there.
Label the worker node:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true <NODE_NAME> Create the resource class /windows-docker-build and the secret windows-docker-build-token.
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
docker stack deploy -c windows\stack\runners.yaml -c windows\stack\docker-build.yaml runners Jobs can build Windows images only, because the engine runs in Windows-container mode. The file examples/windows-docker-build.yml has a job. Keep registry credentials for docker login and docker push in a restricted context.
data.pattern-a-the-host-docker-engine#Pattern:
A service of this class bind-mounts the engine endpoint of the node: /var/run/docker.sock on Linux, and the named pipe \\.\pipe\docker_engine on Windows.
Caution The engine endpoint is root-equivalent on its node (administrator-equivalent on Windows). A job that can use it can start a privileged container, mount any host path, and read the data of other jobs and containers. Use pattern A only for trusted projects, on a dedicated node.
Four controls limit the damage:
Worker nodes only. The service runs only where node.role == worker. On a manager the socket also controls the Swarm, so a job could read the token of every class. A single-node Swarm has only a manager, so do not use pattern A there. Labeled nodes only. The service runs only on nodes with machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true. Every other service carries != true, so labeling a node moves the other classes off it. No neighbors. The engine shows every container on the node. Refer to Keep the docker-build node to itself. Trusted projects only. Restrict the class with a config policy, and keep production contexts away from it (CircleCI-side controls). State persists: the images, containers, volumes, and build cache of the host engine outlive the job, and nothing else prunes this engine. Remove what a job creates in a final step, and schedule docker builder prune and docker image prune on the node (Free disk space). Never run docker volume prune there: the node also holds the volume runner-bin.
data.pattern-b-rootless-buildkit-on-the-host#: Run a rootless BuildKit daemon on the host under a dedicated unprivileged account, and mount only its socket into a runner service. Jobs send builds to it with a BuildKit client. The daemon exposes the build API, not the Docker API, so a job cannot start arbitrary containers or mount host paths. The risk shrinks but stays: the daemon shares the host kernel, and every job shares its build cache. Machine runner swarm has no stack file, helper, or test for it.
data.pattern-c-a-daemonless-builder-in-the-jo: Run a daemonless builder inside the job container, such as a maintained fork of Kaniko or Buildah. Nothing of the host is exposed. These builders have their own privilege needs: rootless Buildah relies on user namespaces, and Kaniko expects to run as root inside its container. Swarm ignores security_opt and privileged in a stack file, so test your builder in a class that matches your policy first. This repository has no stack file or test for it.
data.what-to-avoid#What to avoid: Mounting the Docker socket into any class that is not dedicated to builds. Starting a privileged Docker-in-Docker container from a job. Swarm ignores privileged, and it is root-equivalent where it works. Running pattern A on a manager, or on a node that also runs production workloads.

data: The stack files run stock images and mount the runner into them, so the image of a class is the environment its jobs see. Machine runner swarm publishes no class image. Its one image, the token proxy, holds the class tokens and is no environment for a job (The token proxy image). This page covers the stock images and how to bring your own on each OS.
data.linux-bring-your-own-image#Linux: bring:
Build an image when jobs need tools that you do not want to install in every job. This is also how a hardened class gets tools, because jobs there have no sudo.
linux/images/example/Dockerfile starts from a cimg image and adds postgresql-client. Copy it and replace the packages.
docker build -t registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 linux/images/example docker push registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 Then set the image of a service in your stack file:
image: registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 Every node that runs the service must be able to pull the image (Registry needs). Rebuild when the base changes, for example once a month.
The Dockerfile adds tools and nothing of the runner. Its USER circleci only affects a plain docker run: the stack starts the container as root so that the entrypoint can create users.
data.linux-stock-images-with-the-mounted-runn:
The statically linked runner lives in the per-node volume runner-bin, which the runner-distributor service fills. The stack mounts it read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm in every container, with current pointing to the active version. The entrypoint, a Swarm config mounted at /circleci-runner-entrypoint, starts as root, checks the runner against its SHA-256 record, prepares the users, and runs the runner as circleci-runner.
The image contains none of the runner, so a new runner version needs no image rebuild and no restart (The runner distributor on Linux, Upgrade the runner on Linux).
Service File Image linux-default runners.yaml cimg/base:2026.10 linux-java classes-extra.yaml cimg/openjdk:21.0 linux-hardened classes-extra.yaml cimg/base:2026.10
data.pin-the-image#Pin the image:
Tags such as 21.0 move when the publisher rebuilds the image. Pin production services by digest and update them on a schedule:
image: cimg/base:2026.10@sha256: docker buildx imagetools inspect cimg/base:2026.10
data.private-certificate-authorities#Private:
The runner, its task agent, and the job steps read the certificate store of the image of their class. To trust a private authority (an inspecting proxy, your CircleCI server, a private registry, or a package host), put it in an image of your own. The stack files need no change. This repository does not test it.
On Linux, add the certificate to the system store, in a Dockerfile on top of your image:
FROM cimg/base:2026.10@sha256:
data.what-an-image-needs#What an image needs:
Requirement Why Linux, any C library The runner is statically linked. It runs unmodified in cimg/base, cimg/openjdk, Alpine, and UBI minimal sudo, or util-linux setpriv Steps each job down to the job user. The hardened class (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false) needs util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo setpriv or su Starts the runner as circleci-runner useradd or adduser Creates circleci-runner, and the job user when the image has none sed, grep, stat, install, getent, id, cut, tr, chmod, env, sha256sum, readlink, sleep Used by the entrypoint. BusyBox and coreutils both provide them wget or curl, tar, awk, mktemp, mv, chown Only for a microVM class, whose entrypoint downloads the runner The cimg images have everything. Alpine has only the BusyBox su, and UBI minimal has neither sudo nor setpriv. The tests run the entrypoint in cimg/base, cimg/openjdk, Alpine 3 (with sudo and with setpriv), and UBI 9 minimal. Add missing packages in a derived image:
Base Add Debian and Ubuntu apt-get install sudo Alpine apk add sudo setpriv UBI minimal microdnf install sudo util-linux (util-linux-core is not enough) The entrypoint exits with code 80 and names the missing packages. The end-to-end CI jobs run real jobs through the sudo path (default class) and the setpriv --no-new-privs path (hardened class).
The job user is circleci by default. Set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER to another existing account. If the account does not exist, the entrypoint creates it with uid 2001, with passwordless sudo while MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO is true and the image has sudo. The image environment (PATH, JAVA_HOME, LANG, proxy variables) reaches the jobs. The runner token does not.
data.windows-bring-your-own-image#Windows: br:
Add tools in an image on top of stock Server Core. The host still provides the runner and Git through the mounts, and the stack file still sets entrypoint and the full PATH, so add the directory of your tool to that PATH.
windows/images/example/Dockerfile adds Node.js from the official zip, pinned by version and SHA-256. Copy it and swap the tool, keeping the pattern:
Start FROM the stock Server Core image of your host’s tag. Download a pinned release, and verify its SHA-256 checksum before you use it. Install the tool in a fixed directory, and add that directory to the PATH of the service in windows\stack\custom-image.yaml. Check that the tool runs. Leave USER alone: the runner needs ContainerAdministrator, which creates symbolic links for the task agent. Do not put PsExec64.exe on the PATH of the image or of the service: the task agent would switch to a desktop wrapper that containers cannot run.
Build the example from the root of the repository (the build context is the windows directory):
docker build -f windows/images/example/Dockerfile --build-arg WINDOWS_TAG=ltsc2022 -t machine-runner-swarm-windows-example:ltsc2022 windows Push the result to a registry that every Windows node can pull from, because Swarm does not share local images. Then set the image of the windows-custom service in the add-on stack file windows\stack\custom-image.yaml, create the resource class and the secret windows-custom-token, and deploy with -c windows\stack\runners.yaml -c windows\stack\custom-image.yaml. The file examples/windows-custom-image.yml has a job on that class. Rebuild when the base image or a tool changes.
data.windows-stock-server-core-with-mounts#Wi:
The default Windows service runs the unmodified Microsoft Server Core image, for example mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022. Two read-only mounts of the per-node volume runner-bin, which runner-distributor-windows fills, add what the runner needs:
Volume path (volume.subpath) Container path Content current C:\machine-runner-swarm bin\circleci-runner.exe, the record SHA256, and VERSION git\current C:\Program Files\Git Portable Git for Windows: git, bash, sh, tar, gzip, ssh current and git\current are relative directory symbolic links, to versions\ and to the pinned Git, which the distributor moves. Docker resolves a link when it creates a container, so a new runner version reaches the next container only, and a running job keeps its version. Docker refuses a junction or an absolute link in a subpath (Upgrade the runner on Windows).
The runner is the main process: the service sets entrypoint to C:\machine-runner-swarm\bin\circleci-runner.exe machine --config C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml. It also sets the full PATH, because a PATH in the service environment replaces the one of the image. Git for Windows comes after the Windows directories, so the Windows find, sort, and tar stay first.
The Git mount is read-only, so the service sets Git options through the environment: GIT_CONFIG_COUNT, GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0, and GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0 enable core.longpaths, and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GCM_INTERACTIVE=never stop prompts that nothing in a container can answer.
Pin the image with a digest, and redeploy when Microsoft republishes the tag (each Patch Tuesday).
docker buildx imagetools inspect mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 Nano Server is not supported. Windows images must match the host build (Image tags and host builds).

data:
In a Kata Containers microVM, every container starts in a small virtual machine with its own Linux kernel, so a job that breaks out of its container reaches the guest, not the node. The optional add-on stack file linux/stack/microvm.yaml runs two resource classes this way, and the default classes do not change.
Use it when jobs need a boundary stronger than a container, or privileges that are unsafe on a shared kernel. linux-microvm-docker runs its own Docker daemon inside the VM, so an image build needs no host Docker socket. That is safer than the docker-build class. It builds images only: docker run, Compose and service containers do not work in it (Run Docker inside the VM).
Warning Status: experimental. The classes ship and stay in the stack. Maturity:
Tested by the CI (linux/tests/microvm.sh): placement, DNS, the claim through the token proxy, the runner download and its verification, the rolling update, and builds with the Docker daemon in the VM. On amd64, with Kata 4.2.0, Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU, in nested virtualization on AWS, against a fake CircleCI API. Verified by hand only: one real CircleCI job ran. CI runs an empty task, with no checkout, caches, workspaces or artifacts through the task agent. Run a real job on a node of your own before you depend on it. Not tested: arm64, AMD CPUs, other clouds, Firecracker, many VMs at once, out-of-memory behavior, and Kata upgrades under load. Refer to What is tested.
data.configure-docker#Configure Docker:
Add the runtimes to /etc/docker/daemon.json and make Kata the default. Merge these keys into the file if it exists. The runtime kata uses Cloud Hypervisor. The runtime kata-qemu is the fallback. The test suite runs this exact block.
{ "default-runtime": "kata", "runtimes": { "kata": { "runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2", "options": {"ConfigPath": "/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-clh-runtime-rs.toml"} }, "kata-qemu": { "runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2", "options": {"ConfigPath": "/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml"} } } } Restart Docker, then check that a container has its own kernel. The two kernels must differ. Containers that ran before the restart stay as they are.
sudo systemctl restart docker uname -r docker run --rm alpine uname -r QEMU as the fallback. Set "default-runtime": "kata-qemu" if Cloud Hypervisor does not work on your hardware. QEMU backs the memory of every VM with /dev/shm, which must hold the memory of all VMs together (half of the RAM by default). A tmpfs that is too small fails with kvm run failed Bad address and a vsock timeout. In a Docker-in-Docker container, as in the tests, start it with --shm-size=16g.
Label the node before you deploy the stack. A Kata node without the label still matches microvm-dns, which cannot work in a VM.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true
data.deploy-the-classes#Deploy the classes:
Create the resource classes /linux-microvm and /linux-microvm-docker, and the secrets linux-microvm-token and linux-microvm-docker-token, which go to token-proxy only (Resource classes). Delete a class you do not want from your copy of the stack file, with its secret and network.
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
docker stack deploy -c linux/stack/runners.yaml -c linux/stack/microvm.yaml runners The classes run the same entrypoint as linux-default. A VM has the CPUs of the class limit plus one, and the memory of the limit: cpus: "2" and memory: 4G give a VM with 3 CPUs and about 3.9 GB. Without a limit, a VM gets 1 CPU and 2 GiB. Set limits and reservations for the VM you want (what it costs).
The file examples/linux-microvm.yml has a job for each class.
data.dns#DNS:
Docker’s embedded DNS server, 127.0.0.11, cannot be reached from inside a Kata VM. microvm.yaml works around it in two parts:
The forwarder. microvm-dns runs CoreDNS with forward . 127.0.0.11 on a node without the microvm label and joins the networks of both classes, so token-proxy and service names resolve. It is published on port 53, TCP and UDP, through the routing mesh. The node file. The stack mounts a file of each microVM node read-only at /etc/resolv.conf of every job. It names the gateway of docker_gwbridge (the node itself), and the routing mesh sends the query on to a forwarder. Write the node file, after the node joined the Swarm. The gateway is 172.18.0.1 by default and differs when that range was taken, so read it from Docker:
sudo install -d /etc/machine-runner-swarm gw=$(docker network inspect docker_gwbridge --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}') printf 'nameserver %s
' "$gw" | sudo tee /etc/machine-runner-swarm/microvm-resolv.conf Without this file the task does not start (the bind mount fails), so a node that skipped this step never runs a class with broken DNS.
Create the Corefile config once, on a manager. Swarm configs are immutable: to change the Corefile, create a config under a new name and change microvm-corefile in your copy of the stack file.
printf '.:53 {
 errors
 forward . 127.0.0.11
 cache 30
}
' | docker config create microvm-corefile - Warning The routing mesh opens port 53 on every interface of every node, so the forwarder is an open resolver for anyone who can reach the node. Close port 53 to the outside with your cloud firewall or security group, and open it only between the nodes. Docker bypasses ufw and firewalld for published ports, so use the DOCKER-USER chain to filter on the node. A node that runs its own DNS server on port 53 loses it to the routing mesh.
Internal names. The forwarder uses the resolvers of its own node. A name that only the microVM nodes resolve, such as an internal mirror, fails in the VM. Use a name the runc node resolves, or an IP address in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL. Only microVM nodes. Replace forward . 127.0.0.11 with forward . 1.1.1.1 (or your resolver) and put microvm-dns on that node without the constraint. Public names then resolve, and service names do not.
data.how-it-works#How it works:
Swarm cannot ask for Kata per service. The Docker daemon of each node picks the runtime, so the node decides:
A microVM node has Kata as the default-runtime of its Docker daemon and the label machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true. Every container on it is a microVM. The two classes run only on nodes with that label. Every other class carries node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.microvm != true, so labeling a node moves them off it. The classes set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_REQUIRE_MICROVM=true. The entrypoint exits with code 80 unless /proc/cmdline names kata-containers, so a node with the label but the wrong default runtime never runs a class that has SYS_ADMIN. Docker’s embedded DNS does not work in a Kata VM, so the service microvm-dns forwards it (DNS). The classes claim through the token proxy, which runs on a runc node. A job in a VM never sees a class token. Each container downloads and verifies the runner (The runner in a VM), and the global service microvm-netkeep keeps the class networks up (Rolling updates). linux-default linux-microvm linux-microvm-docker Kernel of the job The node kernel Its own guest kernel Its own guest kernel Runs on Nodes without the microvm and docker-build labels Nodes with microvm=true Nodes with microvm=true Job user circleci, with sudo circleci, with sudo circleci, with sudo Class token in the job No, the proxy holds it No No The runner The per-node volume, read-only Downloaded by the container, then verified Downloaded by the container, then verified Capabilities Docker’s defaults, minus NET_RAW and MKNOD The same Docker’s defaults, plus SYS_ADMIN (no NET_ADMIN, and NET_RAW stays) Replicas 2 2 1, and keep it at 1 (Security) Docker in the job No No Its own dockerd in the VM, on a tmpfs, for builds
data.nested-virtualization-in-the-cloud#Neste: Cloud Instances Notes AWS C8i, M8i, R8i (also the flex sizes), C7i, M7i, R7i (also the flex sizes), I7i, and every .metal size Intel only. Enable nested virtualization when you launch the instance. The tested node was an r8i-flex.2xlarge Google Cloud, Azure, and others Nested virtualization exists on some families Untested CircleCI’s own cloud executors do not offer nested virtualization, except the Android machine image. Refer to CI.
data.requirements#Requirements: KVM. The node needs /dev/kvm: bare metal, or a virtual machine with nested virtualization. Linux amd64. The add-on pins the amd64 build of Kata 4.2.0. Docker Engine 24 or later, and a Swarm that follows Multi-node clusters. One runc node at least for microvm-dns and token-proxy, for example a manager. A Swarm whose only node is a microVM node cannot run them (DNS). The base stack runners.yaml with its placeholder secret (Install on Linux). The token proxy never runs on a microVM node: label its node as Multi-node clusters says. A node of its own. The default runtime applies to every container, so a microVM node runs microVM classes only. Egress to circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, the host the task agent already comes from (Egress hosts).
data.rolling-updates#Rolling updates:
Docker removes an overlay network from a node when its last container leaves. A Kata container that starts in that gap stays in the Created state for good, and Swarm retries with a new task that hangs the same way. A restart after a finished job is safe (Swarm waits delay: 10s first). A rolling update is not: update_config stops the old container and starts the new one at once (order: stop-first).
microvm-netkeep closes the gap: one small VM sleeps on every microVM node, attached to both class networks, so the overlays never go away. Keep the service in your copy of the stack file. Without it, drain a node before an update, and use docker service update --force only when the service has a replica on another node.
data.run-docker-inside-the-vm#Run Docker insi:
A job on linux-microvm-docker starts its own Docker daemon in the VM and builds with it. No socket of the node is involved. The class has SYS_ADMIN and no NET_ADMIN, and a 6 GiB tmpfs at /var/lib/docker, because overlayfs cannot sit on the virtiofs root of the VM. Images and the build cache live in the memory of the VM and vanish with the job.
Without NET_ADMIN a job cannot change the address of its container, which the token proxy trusts to tell runners apart. The price: start the daemon with --bridge=none --iptables=false, and build with --network=host.
The VM mounts /sys, /sys/fs/cgroup, and /proc/sys read-only, and the job must remount them before dockerd can start:
sudo mount -o remount,rw /sys sudo mount -o remount,rw /sys/fs/cgroup sudo mount -o remount,rw /proc/sys sudo sh -c 'dockerd --bridge=none --iptables=false > /tmp/dockerd.log 2>&1 &' timeout 60 sh -c 'until sudo docker info > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done' sudo docker build --network=host -t app . Builds work, and so do docker load, docker save, docker create with docker cp, and a push to a registry. Pass --network=host to every build, also in docker buildx build: a Dockerfile cannot ask for it. docker run, Compose and service containers do not work. Starting a container needs NET_ADMIN (failed to create default sandbox: operation not permitted, also with --network=host and --network=none). Use another class for jobs that start containers. To allow it here, add NET_ADMIN to cap_add in your copy of the stack file, keep one replica on its own overlay, and use it for trusted projects only: a job with NET_ADMIN can take over the address of another container. The class keeps NET_RAW. BuildKit starts every RUN step with Docker’s default capabilities, and runc fails with unable to apply caps when the container dropped one. So a job can send raw packets with another source address into its overlay. One replica keeps that harmless (Security). Rootless BuildKit does not work, because file capabilities do not survive virtiofs. A rootful dockerd or buildkitd does.
data.security#Security: What the VM adds. A job that escapes its container, or abuses SYS_ADMIN, lands in a guest kernel and its own root filesystem, not on the node, other jobs, or the tokens of other classes. The VM shares no writable state with other jobs. It does not filter egress, and replicas of a class share an overlay network. Residual risk. A bug in virtiofs, the VMM, or the guest kernel could still reach the node, which runs virtiofsd, a VMM and the Kata shim for every job. Keep Kata and the node kernel current. To isolate linux-microvm-docker further, label nodes machine-runner-swarm.class.linux-microvm-docker=true (Multi-node clusters), add node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.class.linux-microvm-docker == true to its constraints in your copy of the stack file, and != true to those of linux-microvm. Why one replica. The token proxy accepts a claim from an address that Swarm lists for the class. Other classes drop NET_RAW, so a job cannot send packets from another address. linux-microvm-docker keeps it (BuildKit needs it) and has no NET_ADMIN, so a job there can send raw packets but cannot take over an address. With one replica on its own overlay, no other runner is there to impersonate. The stack-config test requires replicas: 1 and SYS_ADMIN as the only added capability. For more builds at once, copy the service under another name and resource class, with its own network, secret and proxy entries (Add a class). Do not raise replicas. The guard. SYS_ADMIN on runc is a host escape. The label and constraints keep linux-microvm-docker on microVM nodes, and the entrypoint check keeps it off a node with the label but not the runtime. The stack-config test requires MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_REQUIRE_MICROVM=true on every service that adds SYS_ADMIN, in every stack file.
data.set-up-a-microvm-node#Set up a microVM n:
Run these steps as root on every microVM node, after it joined the Swarm (Install on Linux).
Check KVM and load the vhost modules. Kata uses vhost_vsock to reach the agent in the VM, and vhost_net for networking.
ls -l /dev/kvm sudo modprobe vhost_vsock vhost_net printf 'vhost_vsock\nvhost_net\n' | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/kata.conf ls -l /dev/vhost-vsock /dev/vhost-net Install Kata 4.2.0. The release tarball is about 1 GB and unpacks to about 2.3 GB in /opt/kata. It needs zstd. Check the SHA-256 before you unpack it.
curl -fLO https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/releases/download/4.2.0/kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst echo 'b828904fa3f1e49ddd7dc799c72cb1503cd1e772d354c3987c8d4189b2a623a8 kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst' | sha256sum -c - sudo tar --zstd -xf kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst -C / sudo ln -sf /opt/kata/runtime-rs/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2 /usr/local/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2 To upgrade, unpack a new release the same way and restart Docker. Running VMs keep the old files until they stop. Without a route to GitHub, copy the tarball in and keep the SHA-256 check.
data.the-runner-in-a-vm#The runner in a VM:
The other classes mount the per-node volume runner-bin read-only. A microVM class does not: root with SYS_ADMIN inside a VM can remount a shared mount read-write, and the write would reach the runner of every later job. So nothing writable is shared:
The entrypoint downloads the runner into the container (sh /runner-distributor.sh --once, a Swarm config of the class): about 22 MB for each job, from the source the task agent comes from. It checks the SHA-256 and the reported version, and writes the same record as on any node. The usual entrypoint checks follow. A mirror of your own must be reachable from the VM (DNS). The settings are those of the distributor, with the same defaults, set as variables of docker stack deploy (they sit in the service, because no distributor serves them). The pin and its SHA-256 values are the same as in runners.yaml: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION: an exact pin by default, or 3.1, 3, current (the version policy). A floating version is resolved in each VM when the job starts and ignores any SHA-256 list. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL (a mirror), and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 (the SHA-256 values of the pin, or manifest, which checks against the manifest and is weaker). A failed or mismatching download ends the container with exit code 80, and Swarm retries after the restart delay of 10 seconds. A job can rewrite the runner binary and its record only in its own copy, which goes away with the VM, and no class token is in the VM. Because nothing is shared, no dedicated nodes are needed for this reason.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause and fix A task is rejected with bind source path does not exist The node file /etc/machine-runner-swarm/microvm-resolv.conf is missing. Write it The class exits with code 80 and not in a Kata microVM The node has the label, and Docker runs runc. Check docker info --format '{{.DefaultRuntime}}' and Configure Docker, or remove the label The class stays Pending with no suitable node No node has machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true. Label the node A job cannot resolve names, or only some queries succeed microvm-dns is not running, the config microvm-corefile is missing (DNS), a replica runs on a Kata node without the label, or another -c file overrides microvm-dns and the merge dropped its UDP port. docker service ls must show *:53->53/tcp, *:53->53/udp for runners_microvm-dns, and docker service ps runners_microvm-dns replicas on nodes without the label. Change the service in your copy of microvm.yaml, not in another -c file A task stays Starting and its container stays Created after an update The overlay left the node while the task started. Check that microvm-netkeep runs on the node, then docker service update --force the class (Rolling updates) A class exits 80 with “cannot download and verify the runner in this microVM” The VM could not download the runner, or its SHA-256 did not match. docker service logs runners_linux-microvm shows the download lines. Check DNS, egress to circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 A container does not start, with ETIMEDOUT on vsock vhost_vsock is not loaded (Set up a microVM node step 1), or QEMU lacks /dev/shm space (Configure Docker) dockerd in the VM fails with read-only file system The job skipped the remounts (Run Docker inside the VM)
data.what-is-not-tested#What is not tested: Real jobs (checkout, caches, workspaces and artifacts over virtiofs with the real task agent: one ran by hand, none run in CI), out-of-memory behavior against the cgroup limit, other clouds, AMD CPUs, arm64, Firecracker (it has no virtiofs), the Go shim of Kata, clusters of more than two nodes, the load of many VMs, Kata upgrades under load, and Windows (next section).
data.what-is-tested#What is tested:
linux/tests/microvm.sh runs two Docker-in-Docker nodes with KVM, the real stack files runners.yaml and microvm.yaml, the real entrypoint, a distributor on the runc node, a test mirror that serves the runner, the token proxy image built from proxy/, and the real runner against a fake API. It skips when /dev/kvm is missing. It checks:
Placement: the classes stay pending until a node has the label, and the Kata node has no runner-bin volume. Isolation: the guest kernel differs from the node kernel, /proc/cmdline names kata-containers, and /etc/resolv.conf is the read-only node file. DNS: public names, token-proxy, and service names resolve through the forwarder. A control without the node file fails. The real runner claims through the real token proxy from inside a VM and runs a task as the job user. The class token is in no file, variable, or process of the VM. The runner download is verified, a root shell that rewrites the binary changes nothing for the next VM, a wrong SHA-256 is refused (exit 80), and a floating version resolves in the VM. A forced rolling update replaces the VM because of microvm-netkeep. A control without it hangs. dockerd starts with --bridge=none --iptables=false, uses overlay2 on the tmpfs, and builds an image with --network=host. The stack-config test pins SYS_ADMIN, no NET_ADMIN, and the replica count. The label on a runc node makes both classes exit 80, and QEMU passes the same checks (SWARM_TEST_KATA_VMM=qemu).
data.what-it-costs#What it costs:
Measured on one r8i-flex.2xlarge (nested KVM), Docker 29.9, Kata 4.2.0, in Docker-in-Docker:
Measure runc Cloud Hypervisor Dragonball Container start 0.27 s 1.16 s 2.5 s Swarm deploy to the first output of the container 1.3 s 3.4 s not measured Memory. microvm-netkeep adds one small VM (256 MB limit) to every microVM node. An idle VM with 2 GiB takes about 160 MB of host memory, and more as the job runs. The tmpfs of linux-microvm-docker counts against the VM memory. CPU. Compute speed equals runc. The reservation covers only the limit, not the extra CPU. Disk. virtiofs makes fsync about twice as slow as on the node’s disk. A tmpfs avoids it. Start-up. A job waits about a second longer for the container, plus a few seconds for the runner download. Dragonball, the built-in VMM of runtime-rs, works with the same steps but starts more slowly, so the docs use Cloud Hypervisor.
data.windows-hyper-v-isolation#Windows: Hyper:
isolation: hyperv runs each Windows container in a lightweight Hyper-V utility VM with its own kernel, instead of the host kernel (isolation: process, the default in windows/stack/runners.yaml). This is untested. A stack file for it would be an add-on like this one, on a host with the Hyper-V role:
services: windows-hyperv: # ... the settings of windows-default in windows/stack/runners.yaml isolation: hyperv It does not need the image to match the host version, but it needs nested virtualization, which CircleCI’s own Windows machines do not offer (--isolation hyperv fails there with “The request is not supported”). On AWS, use the instance families above, or .metal. Test it on your own hosts first.

data: Each Swarm service in a stack file is one CircleCI resource class, named /, and deploy.replicas is how many jobs it runs at once. This page lists the shipped sizes, then how to add a class, choose replicas, run a persistent class, enable Rerun job with SSH, and read the stack variables.
data.choose-replica-counts#Choose replica cou:
deploy.replicas is the number of jobs the class runs at the same time.
Estimate the peak number of parallel jobs for the class. Check that nodes with enough room exist. A replica needs its full reservation on one node. Add one replica for many very short jobs. A replica needs about 10 seconds between jobs. Set deploy.replicas in the stack file and deploy again. The file stays the source of truth. For a quick change, scale the service. The next docker stack deploy resets the count to the file.
docker service scale runners_linux-default=4 Swarm has no autoscaling and this stack adds none. Set replicas: 0 to switch a class off without deleting it, and know that jobs for a class with no runner wait without limit and hold concurrency (Capacity and concurrency). For elastic capacity, use the machine runner orchestrator or CircleCI cloud executors (FAQ).
data.define-a-class#Define a class:
The shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml has one class, linux-default. Add other classes to your copy of the stack files (deploy/runners.yaml, as Install on Linux describes) and deploy your copy. linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml is a worked example: it adds linux-java and linux-hardened.
Create the resource class and a token in CircleCI. The class name must equal the service name.
circleci runner resource-class create /linux-python --org --generate-token Copy the service linux-default in your stack file under another name, and change the name, hostname, CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME and networks as in the example below.
Create the secret -token with the token. Refer to Create the secrets or Create the secrets on Windows.
On Linux, add the class network and secret to the existing token-proxy service. The proxy serves a class for every secret -token that it holds, and finds its runners as tasks..
Deploy again with the same -c files as before. Swarm creates the new service and leaves the others alone.
docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners The runner name must be unique across the runners of your organization. It has at most 64 characters and contains only letters, numbers, ., (, ), _, -, and spaces. A long hostname plus class name can exceed that, and the runner then exits with code 80.
A Linux example, in your copy of runners.yaml, where the anchors *runner, *env, *restart, *update and *placement resolve. First, the service next to linux-default:
services: linux-python: <<: *runner image: cimg/python:3.14 hostname: "{{.Node.Hostname}}-linux-python-{{.Task.Slot}}" environment: <<: *env CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME: "{{.Node.Hostname}}-linux-python-{{.Task.Slot}}" MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "true" networks: [linux-python] cap_drop: [NET_RAW, MKNOD] # keep NET_RAW dropped: the proxy tells runners apart by source address deploy: replicas: 2 restart_policy: *restart update_config: *update resources: limits: {cpus: "2", memory: 4G, pids: 4096} reservations: {cpus: "2", memory: 4G} placement: *placement Second, add these lines to the token-proxy: key, which appears once in the file. Do not repeat the key:
token-proxy: secrets: # ... the secrets of the classes that are there - {source: linux-python-token, target: linux-python-token, uid: "65534", gid: "65534", mode: 0400} networks: [linux-default, linux-python] # every class network, the new one included Third, declare the network (linux-python: {driver: overlay, driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}}) under the top-level networks: and the secret (linux-python-token: {external: true}) under secrets:.
A deploy that adds a class secret replaces the proxy task. What the runners see meanwhile is in Restart the proxy. A class that the proxy does not serve gets 403 on every claim, and the proxy log says not a runner of any class. For a hardened class, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" with the capability settings of linux-hardened (Concepts).
A class in its own stack file. Write token-proxy there with only the secret and network: Swarm merges files by name. Anchors do not reach into another file, so repeat what *runner sets (user: "0", the entrypoint and its config, the placeholder secret runner-placeholder-token, CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080, and the read-only volume runner-bin), or copy classes-extra.yaml. The config name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the file, because a Swarm config cannot change (Upgrade to a new release of this repository).
A class on Windows. Copy a service such as windows-default in your copy of windows\stack\runners.yaml, with its two mounts of the volume runner-bin (subpath: current and subpath: 'git\current'). Its CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME is "{{.Node.Hostname}}-windows--{{.Task.Slot}}", and the file sets no hostname. The secret has no uid, gid, or mode, and the file defines no networks. A single-task class also adds its secret (target -token) to token-proxy-windows, and reads runner-placeholder-token.
data.exit-codes#Exit codes: Code Source Meaning 0 Runner A normal exit after a job or a runner drain. Swarm starts a new container 80 Entrypoint A prerequisite is missing: the link current does not exist after the wait, the runner does not match its SHA-256 record, the runner or a directory above it is not root-owned or is writable, the image has neither sudo nor setpriv (or, for a hardened class, no util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs), MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO is invalid, or the entrypoint cannot remove every sudo right of the job user 80 Runner A configuration error: a missing or invalid name, an empty token, an unknown log level, or an invalid mode 1 Runner The config file is missing because the secret is not attached, the YAML does not parse, or a duration is malformed Swarm restarts a container that exits with any code after 10 seconds. It never gives up and never backs off, so a configuration error repeats until you fix it (Troubleshooting).
data.linux#Linux:
linux/stack/persistent.yaml defines linux-persistent. It sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE: continuous with no idle timeout, mounts the named volume persistent-home at /home/circleci (Swarm copies the image content of that directory into the new volume on first use), and sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false", so each job must clean up what an earlier job left (Working directory cleanup).
A volume lives on one node, so the service has the constraint node.hostname == CHANGE-ME. Edit it in your copy (deploy/persistent.yaml) before you deploy.
The runner keeps its class token in its own container, because a continuous runner claims after every job and the proxy allows one claim for each container. The shipped file sets MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false", so jobs have no sudo and cannot read the token file, and the tools that a job needs must be in the image (Images). Set it to "true" in your copy if jobs need sudo, and accept that a job that uses it reads the token and can run a runner of its own on the class.
printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-persistent-token - docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners Recycle the runner with a forced update. It drains first (it finishes the running job and takes no new one), and the volume survives. A forced update is also how the class moves to a new runner version.
docker service update --force runners_linux-persistent
data.persistent-mode#Persistent mode:
Status: experimental. CI runs the persistent class with a fake or idle runner only, and no real job runs on it in CI.
A persistent class runs the runner in continuous mode. One long-lived container claims job after job, and a named volume keeps data between jobs. Use it only for trusted projects that gain a lot from warm caches.
Warning Continuous mode removes the guarantee of a clean environment. A job can leave files, processes, or settings that later jobs see, and can change what later jobs run. CircleCI rates untrusted jobs on a runner that keeps its environment as the highest risk.
To limit the risk:
Use a separate class restricted to named projects with a config policy (CircleCI-side controls), and keep production contexts away from it. Put cleanup steps at the start of its jobs. The runner does not clean the working directory on Linux. Recycle the runner on a schedule. This class is weaker than the single-task classes: it does not use the token proxy, so the runner holds the real token, and on Windows every job can read it (The persistent class).
data.rerun-job-with-ssh#Rerun job with SSH:
Status: experimental. CI checks that the files parse, merge and keep their contract (the host-mode port 54782, max_replicas_per_node: 1, the advertise address). The Swarm side was proven by hand on Linux with a real runner. No CI test logs in over SSH, and the Windows file is untested.
The add-on files linux/stack/ssh-rerun.yaml and windows\stack\ssh-rerun.yaml define linux-default-ssh and windows-default-ssh. Their runners support Rerun job with SSH, which opens a shell in a running job. The default classes publish no port and cannot serve it.
Advertised address. Setting CIRCLECI_RUNNER_SSH_ADVERTISE_ADDR turns the feature on. The task agent then starts an SSH server on the fixed port 54782, and the Enable SSH and Wait for SSH steps show the address. CircleCI only displays it, so it can be any name or IP address your users reach. The add-on files set {{.Node.Hostname}}:54782. If DNS does not resolve node hostnames, use one that does, for example {{.Node.Hostname}}.example.com:54782. Host-mode port. The file publishes 54782 in host mode, so it opens on the node that runs the task (ingress mode would send a connection to any replica, which can be another user’s job). A node has one port 54782, so the service sets max_replicas_per_node: 1, and replicas beyond the number of eligible nodes stay pending. Which class. A rerun uses the class of the original job, so set the resource_class of the job to debug to /linux-default-ssh. To give an existing class SSH, copy three settings from the add-on file into that service: the environment variable, the host-mode port, and max_replicas_per_node: 1. Every replica of that class then needs its own node. printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-default-ssh-token - docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/ssh-rerun.yaml runners Before you use it:
Firewall. Open inbound TCP 54782 on the nodes that run the class, only from the networks where your users connect, such as a VPN. Docker publishes the port with NAT rules that run before ufw and firewalld rules, so those rules do not restrict it. Filter in the DOCKER-USER chain or with a cloud security group, for example sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER ! -s -p tcp --dport 54782 -j DROP (not tested here). Refer to Listening ports on a node. SSH key. A user adds a public key in their CircleCI user settings, or, with a GitHub or Bitbucket organization, to their VCS account. Without a key, the Enable SSH step does not appear. Refer to Debug jobs with SSH rerun. Concurrency. A rerun holds the runner for up to 2 hours after a user connects (1 hour on the Free plan), or 10 minutes if nobody does. It counts against the concurrency limit of your organization, and the replica takes no other job. A forgotten session blocks the node. Cancel the rerun in the web app or with the CLI when you finish: the container exits and Swarm starts a new one. Security. The SSH user gets the privileges of the job user and can reach what the job reached. Anyone who can start a job on the class can rerun it with SSH, and only the user who reruns gets their keys added. In linux-default-ssh the job user keeps sudo, so the SSH user is root in the container, but it holds only the placeholder, because the class claims through the token proxy. Set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO to "false" to take root away. Keep the class for named projects and deploy contexts away from it (CircleCI-side controls). On Windows, the SSH user must name the shell: ssh -p 54782 -- powershell.exe. Open the port in Windows Defender Firewall as well.
data.size-the-limits#Size the limits:
Limits cap what a runner can use. Reservations tell the scheduler how much room a replica needs, and the stack sets them equal. A reservation is held whether or not the replica runs a job, so you pay for the peak. A service with no reservation still has the limit shown.
Service File Replicas Reserved for each replica Limit, when it differs linux-default runners.yaml 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB token-proxy runners.yaml 1 0.1 CPU, 32 MB 0.5 CPU, 128 MB runner-distributor runners.yaml One for each Linux node Nothing 0.5 CPU, 256 MB linux-java classes-extra.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-hardened classes-extra.yaml 1 2 CPUs, 4 GB linux-docker-build docker-build.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-microvm microvm.yaml 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB The VM adds overhead of its own, not measured here linux-microvm-docker microvm.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB The same microvm-dns microvm.yaml 2 Nothing 0.5 CPU, 128 MB microvm-netkeep microvm.yaml One for each microVM node Nothing 0.2 CPU, 256 MB linux-persistent persistent.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-default-ssh ssh-rerun.yaml 1 2 CPUs, 4 GB windows-default runners.yaml (Windows) 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB token-proxy-windows runners.yaml (Windows) 1 Nothing 1 CPU, 512 MB runner-distributor-windows runners.yaml (Windows) One for each Windows node Nothing 1 CPU, 1 GB windows-custom, windows-docker-build, windows-default-ssh Add-on files (Windows) 1 each 2 CPUs, 4 GB windows-persistent persistent.yaml (Windows) 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB The shipped runners.yaml reserves 4.1 CPUs and a little over 8 GB on Linux, and 4 CPUs and 8 GB on Windows, before the operating system, Docker and the distributor. classes-extra.yaml adds 6 CPUs and 12 GB.
Setting Linux Windows limits.cpus Caps CPU Caps CPU. A value above the CPU count of the host is rejected limits.memory Caps memory. The kernel kills a job that exceeds it Caps memory limits.pids Caps processes. The files set 4096 Rejected by the Windows engine, so absent reservations Scheduler only. Extra replicas stay pending instead of overcommitting Scheduler only. The engine never receives it ulimits nofile 65536, core 0 Rejected by the Windows engine, so absent Size one runner for the largest job of the class. A job cannot pick a size, so create a second class (for example linux-large) for bigger jobs. The reservations of all replicas on a node must fit in it, with room for the operating system and Docker (for example one CPU and 2 GB). Replicas that do not fit stay Pending.
Swarm cannot limit disk. Jobs share the Docker data disk of the node, so size it for the replicas plus the stopped containers that Swarm keeps (Start Swarm). A Windows node also holds the servercore base image (about 2.2 GB compressed).
Cost. This project has no price of its own. You pay for the nodes at the peak, your CircleCI plan, and the network and storage that jobs use. Runner compute does not use credits, but at least one credit is needed, and self-hosted runner concurrency is a separate limit of your plan (Run jobs on self-hosted runners).
data.stack-keys-on-windows#Stack keys on Wind:
Not every key of a stack file reaches a Windows container.
Effect Keys Used isolation, bind mounts of directories, npipe mounts, named volumes (a volume.subpath may be a relative directory symbolic link, but not a junction or an absolute link), Swarm configs with an absolute target, secrets without uid, gid, and mode, stop_grace_period, logging, entrypoint, environment with Swarm placeholders, labels, deploy.mode: global, deploy.placement, deploy.restart_policy, deploy.update_config, deploy.endpoint_mode, and deploy.resources.limits for cpus and memory Scheduler only deploy.resources.reservations. The engine rejects a memory reservation, so Swarm never sends it Rejected by the Windows engine deploy.resources.limits.pids and ulimits, so the files do not set them. A limits.cpus above the CPU count of the host is rejected too No effect init, cap_drop, cap_add, read_only, tmpfs, and sysctls Ignored by docker stack deploy on every platform security_opt, privileged, userns_mode, restart, and build Three choices in the Windows files follow:
No hostname. A Windows computer name has at most 15 characters, and a templated hostname would give every container of a slot the same COMPUTERNAME. Without it, COMPUTERNAME is the container ID. endpoint_mode: dnsrr. Nothing connects to a runner, so no virtual IP is needed. Settings repeated per service. YAML merge keys do not merge deeply. The idle timeout is set for each service, because the persistent class must not have one, and windows-docker-build repeats the PATH with C:\docker appended. The log driver is json-file with rotation. The local driver also works on Windows.
data.the-secret#The secret: Linux, token proxy: secret -token, target -token, at /run/secrets/-token in the proxy, uid 65534, gid 65534, mode 0400. Linux, persistent runner and placeholder: secret -token (a proxied class uses runner-placeholder-token), target circleci_runner_config.yaml, at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml, uid 2000, gid 2000, mode 0400. Windows: secret -token, target circleci_runner_config.yaml, at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml. Windows supports no owner or mode: administrators and SYSTEM only. The content is api: and auth_token: (the placeholder holds a dummy token). The proxy also accepts a bare token. The entrypoint passes --config to the runner, and environment variables override the file.
data.variables-in-the-stack-files#Variables i: Variable Value in the files Applies to Notes CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME "{{.Node.Hostname}}--{{.Task.Slot}}" Every service Required. Unique per replica CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE single-task, or continuous for persistent classes Every service single-task gives a new container for every job CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT 1h Single-task services An idle replica exits and Swarm replaces it. Do not set it in continuous mode CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR "false" on Linux, "true" on Windows Every service On Linux the runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns, so never set true there (Working directory cleanup) CIRCLECI_RUNNER_LOGGING_FORMAT text Every service No color codes in logs CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MAX_RUN_TIME Commented out, default 5h Every service If you lower it, set stop_grace_period to the same value plus 5 minutes HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY Commented out Every service Jobs inherit them MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO "true" or "false" Linux "false" makes the class hardened CIRCLECI_RUNNER_WORK_DIR, CIRCLECI_RUNNER_TASK_AGENT_DIRECTORY C:\cci\w, C:\cci\agent Windows Job working directory and task agent directory MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID {{.Task.ID}} Windows Lets a job tell which container it ran in GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT, GCM_INTERACTIVE, GIT_CONFIG_* 0, never, and core.longpaths=true Windows Stop Git prompts, and allow long paths PATH The full Server Core path, then Git Windows stock services Replaces the image PATH, so the file spells it out Refer to the machine runner 3 configuration reference for every other CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable. Environment variables override the config file.
data.variables-read-by-the-linux-entrypoint#V:
Variable Default Notes MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT 120 Seconds that the entrypoint waits for the link current of the distributor. Without it, the container exits with code 80 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER circleci The account that runs jobs. The entrypoint creates it with uid 2001 when the image has none MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO true false removes every sudo right of the job user and steps jobs down with setpriv --no-new-privs, which needs util-linux setpriv in the image. Any other value, or a missing setpriv, exits with code 80 The runner user is circleci-runner with uid 2000. It owns the secret file and has no sudo rights.
The entrypoint always sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX: ["sudo","-niHu","","--"], or a setpriv command when the image has no sudo, and always a setpriv --no-new-privs command in a hardened class. It keeps a value that you set for three more: CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR (default false), CIRCLECI_RUNNER_TASK_AGENT_DIRECTORY (default /var/lib/circleci-runner/agent, owned by the runner user) and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_WORK_DIR (default /var/opt/circleci/workdir, owned by the job user; keep a custom directory under /var/opt/circleci).
Arguments that you pass to the entrypoint replace the default command, machine --config /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml.
data.variables-read-by-the-runner-distributor:
These are docker stack deploy variables. x-distributor-env in linux/stack/runners.yaml passes them to the runner-distributor service only. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux.
Variable Default Effect MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION An exact version, the newest that CI tests An exact version pins it. 3.1, 3 and current follow the manifest of CircleCI (the version policy) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR 3 The major version that current may adopt MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL 24h How often a floating version asks the manifest again, and how often an installed pin is checked against its record: seconds, or a number with s, m, h, or d MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner Where manifest.json and the tarballs are, for example a mirror. It must be https://, unless a SHA-256 list is set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 The tarball SHA-256 values of the pinned version A comma-separated list for an exact pin. manifest means no list: the hash of the manifest is trusted, which is weaker. A floating value ignores any list MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP Not set true accepts an http:// download base without a SHA-256 list, for a lab
data.windows#Windows:
windows\stack\persistent.yaml defines windows-persistent. It sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE: continuous with no idle timeout, and mounts the named volume windows-persistent-cache at C:\cache. Point NuGet, npm, and similar caches there with an environment variable in the job. The runner and the jobs use the same account, so the runner cleans the working directory and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR stays "true".
The service is pinned to nodes with the label machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true. Create the secret windows-persistent-token, label the node, and deploy your copy with your copy of the main file:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true <NODE_NAME> docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\persistent.yaml runners

data: CI/CD: What the pipeline tests and when, the maintainer tasks and settings it needs, how the docs site is built, and how releases are signed and published. Releasing: How a merge to main becomes a signed GitHub release, how maintainers enable publishing, and how to recover from a failed release. Contributing: How to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request for machine runner swarm, a CircleCI Labs project.

The pipeline lints everything, tests the Linux and Windows Swarm stacks, and proves with real CircleCI jobs that every job gets a fresh container. From main only it publishes the token proxy image and makes the signed releases (Releasing). Scan reports and logs are job artifacts.
Setup config: .circleci/config.yml Pipeline: .circleci/continue.yml E2E helpers and their simulation: ci/ Lint settings, in the repository root: .hadolint.yaml, .yamllint.yaml, .shellcheckrc, PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1, .trivyignore, lychee.toml
data.a-pull-request-that-needs-a-checksum#A p:
Renovate cannot compute a SHA-256. For a tool pinned with one (Hugo, lychee, the CircleCI CLI, git-cliff, cosign, gh, Go, Kata, PortableGit, 7-Zip, Node.js), the pull request changes the version only, carries the label checksum and a note, and its CI fails on the checksum. To finish it:
Take the new value from the checksums file of the release (the table in Pinned tools names the file), or download the asset and run sha256sum on it. Replace the old value next to the version, in the same branch, and push. For PortableGit, also set Version (X.Y.Z.N for the tag vX.Y.Z.windows.N) and run ci/config-names.sh --write: the distributor is a Swarm config. Update the version in the prose that names it (Releasing, docs/microvm.md for Kata).
data.a-ruleset-for-main#A ruleset for main:
A push to main publishes the token proxy image, makes a release and writes gh-pages, and the scalable-machine-runner-docs context holds a token with Contents: Read and write on the whole repository, so a job of main could push to main itself. A ruleset is a GitHub setting that the repository files cannot enforce or show, and the release signature is only as good as it (What the release trust depends on). The maintainers have set the ruleset below on main (Settings, Rules, Rulesets, New branch ruleset, target: the default branch). Check the settings shows how to read it back.
Require a pull request before merging. The release job never pushes a commit to main. Required code owner review adds nothing while .github/CODEOWNERS is the single line *.
Block force pushes and restrict deletions.
No bypass list, not even for administrators.
Require status checks to pass, with ONE check: the status of the workflow ci. GitHub gets one status per workflow, not per job, so a job name (lint-shell, linux-swarm-a) cannot be required. The setup workflow has a different name per branch (setup-e2e, setup-plain, setup-scan), so requiring one blocks the other branches. ci is on every pipeline, docs-only included, and ends red when any job in it fails. Find the exact status name in a recent commit:
