data.what-a-release-contains#What a release c: Asset Content machine-runner-swarm-.tar.gz README.md, LICENSE, SECURITY.md, VERSION, the generated CHANGELOG.md, docs/, examples/, linux/ and windows/ machine-runner-swarm-.zip The same files, for Windows users SHA256SUMS The SHA-256 checksum of both bundles SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json The cosign bundle: signature, certificate and transparency log entry The bundles come from git archive, so only tracked files ship. They leave out linux/tests/, windows/tests/, docs/ci.md, docs/releasing.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, ci/, .circleci/, proxy/ and site/. ci/bundle-links.py turns every link from a shipped page to a left-out file into a link to that file on GitHub at the release tag (https://github.com///blob/vX.Y.Z/...), and stops the release when a link is dead in the repository too. ci/tests/bundle-links.sh tests it in lint-circleci.
data.what-happens-on-merge#What happens on me:
The setup phase (.circleci/config.yml) passes release: true when the branch is main, both e2e tokens are present, and a commit of the push would make a release (cliff.toml). That switches on every suite, full-suite, e2e-linux, e2e-windows and strict. Otherwise it passes release: false, because a release must wait for every test. The release job requires every other job of the ci workflow except three optional ones. If one fails, nothing is released. The job runs in the serial group /release. When a newer pipeline’s release job waits in the group, the older one skips and the newer one releases both changes. ci/release.sh checks the Swarm config names (Swarm config names) and the runner pin, computes the version and notes, pins the pipeline’s token proxy image digest in the bundle’s stack files, builds the bundles, signs SHA256SUMS and verifies the signature. It then verifies the image signature, gives the image its release tags, and creates the GitHub release, which creates the tag. When the job publishes, it records two Deploys in CircleCI: machine-runner-swarm in github-releases (version the tag), and token-proxy-image in docker-hub (version X.Y.Z). A deploy ends as SUCCESS, or FAILED when a step fails (Deploys). A release needs the image of its commit. proxy-image-publish of the same pipeline pushes it as sha-<12 characters>, and the release requires that job. Without DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN in the context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub (Docker Hub context), a pipeline that is not the production main stays green and publishes nothing: the release job stores the bundle as an artifact and creates no GitHub release. On the production main the same gap fails the jobs (Publishing fails closed on main).
Other branches and tag pipelines never release. A push to main that changes only documentation has no e2e and no release job, unless a commit would make a release, such as fix(docs): (Documentation-only changes).
Add a new job to requires of the release job in .circleci/continue.yml. lint-circleci compiles the workflow and fails when a job is missing. Its $optional list is the only exception: linux-mixed-arch (the emulated mixed-architecture test), proxy-image-edge (moves the edge tag after the tests) and docs-site-comment (posts the preview address on a pull request).
data.what-the-release-trust-depends-on#What t:
A valid signature says one thing: a job of this CircleCI project, from the pipeline definition of this repository, ran on refs/heads/main of this repository. The claim holds only as far as the settings below hold. They are settings of GitHub, CircleCI and Docker Hub, not of the repository, so no file can enforce or show them, and ci/release.sh does not check them. The maintainers have set all of them for v0.1.0. Check the settings says how to read them back.
The main-only expression below is the one in Enable publishing step 3. Every context also has a project restriction (this project).
Setting Where It must say Without it Ruleset of main GitHub repository Require a pull request. Block force pushes. Restrict deletions. No bypass list. Required status check: ci (A ruleset for main) A writer could push a change of .circleci/ or ci/release.sh to main, and it would be signed Ruleset of smr-swarm/** GitHub repository Restrict creations and updates, maintainers alone on the bypass list (The e2e context and smr-swarm/*) A writer could print the e2e runner tokens in a public log from an smr-swarm/ branch Context scalable-machine-runner-release CircleCI organization project and the main-only expression Another branch, an SSH rerun or an API pipeline could read the token Context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub CircleCI organization The same two restrictions (The Docker Hub context) A branch could push the image that the stack files name Context scalable-machine-runner-docs CircleCI organization The same two restrictions A branch could read a token that can write to the repository Context scalable-machine-runner-e2e CircleCI organization project, and the main-only expression with (pipeline.git.branch == "main" or pipeline.git.branch starts-with "smr-swarm/") in place of the branch test A branch could read the e2e runner tokens Context scalable-machine-runner-pr-comments CircleCI organization project, and the main-only expression without the branch test. Any branch pusher can read it, so its token has the least permission (Docs site previews) An SSH rerun or an API pipeline could read it Project settings CircleCI project and organization Build forked pull requests, Pass secrets to builds from forked pull requests, Auto-cancel redundant workflows, SSH reruns and pipelines with an unversioned config: all off (Secrets and public logs) A fork or an API pipeline could run a config of its own Tokens GitHub, Docker Hub Release and docs tokens: fine-grained, this repository only, Contents: Read and write. Comment token: Issues: Read and write, of a bot account. Docker Hub token: read and write on ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy only, from an account with two-factor authentication (What each job can see) A leaked token would reach more than the job that needs it Two things are not covered. The signature does not say that anyone reviewed the change (the ruleset sets the number of reviews, and .github/CODEOWNERS asks the same people for every path), and it says nothing about main before the ruleset existed.
data.where-the-signature-of-the-image-is-stor:
cosign 3.1.3 stores an image signature as a Sigstore bundle, pushed as an OCI 1.1 referrer of the signed digest. cosign verify and cosign download signature fall back to the older sha256-.sig tag only when they find no referrer (the source of no signatures found). ci/proxy-image.sh pins the format with --new-bundle-format=true on both commands (the variable cosign_storage). The flag is the default of 3.1.3 and deprecated: when a cosign version drops it, the rehearsal of the pull request that updates cosign fails, and main does not.
Docker Hub probably does not list a referrer at once: the first run on main failed with no signatures found right after cosign sign. verify_signature therefore tries up to six times, waiting 5, 10, 15, 25 and 35 seconds between tries (SIGN_VERIFY_DELAYS sets the waits). Every check stays whole in every try: identity, issuer, and the ref refs/heads/main on every signature. A signature that names another ref fails at once. After the last failed try, the job prints cosign tree of the digest and the repository tags that start with sha256-.

data.can-a-fork-pull-request-use-these-runner: No. CircleCI does not make self-hosted runners available to a public project that has Build forked pull requests enabled. Keep that setting off for any project that uses these classes. For a private project, a collaborator’s branch runs your code on the node, so restrict each class to the projects that need it (CircleCI-side controls).
data.can-a-job-read-the-runner-token#Can a jo: Class Can a job read the class token? Linux, single-task No, with or without sudo. The runner holds a placeholder and the token proxy holds the token Windows, single-task No test asserts it. A hostile job on the proxy’s host can reach it (Windows) Linux, persistent No by default (no sudo). With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "true", yes Windows, persistent Yes, every job A job that escapes onto the proxy’s node reads every token. Use BitLocker, one token for each class and host, and rotate tokens. A holder of a token can run a rogue runner on that class. See Token model on each OS.
data.can-i-run-a-long-lived-runner-with-warm-: Yes, with a persistent class. It gives up the clean environment, so use it only for trusted projects. The shipped Linux persistent class gives jobs no sudo by default. Refer to Persistent mode.
data.can-i-use-rerun-job-with-ssh#Can I use R: Yes, with the add-on file ssh-rerun.yaml, which defines linux-default-ssh (windows-default-ssh on Windows). A rerun uses the class of the original job, so the job to debug must run on that class. It is experimental: the Swarm side was proven by hand, no CI test logs in over SSH, and the Windows file is untested. Refer to Rerun job with SSH.
data.can-it-run-docker-executor-jobs#Can it r: As a prototype, yes. The classes of machine runner swarm run jobs with machine: true. Container mode adds a Swarm service on each opted-in Linux node that runs jobs with a docker: list and its service containers, as container runner does on Kubernetes. It has no SSH reruns and no Docker layer caching, and it has not yet run against the real CircleCI API. A resource class serves one mode, so give container mode its own classes and tokens. For production Docker executor jobs today, use container runner.
data.do-i-need-to-open-inbound-ports#Do I nee: No. Runners connect outbound over HTTPS, and the shipped classes publish no ports. Only the optional SSH add-on publishes port 54782 (Rerun job with SSH). Multi-node clusters need the Swarm ports between nodes (Inter-node ports).
data.do-proxies-and-custom-certificate-author:
The stack sets nothing for them, and nothing tests them.
Proxy. Set HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY under environment of the service. Jobs inherit them. On Linux, also set HTTPS_PROXY on token-proxy, which calls runner.circleci.com for the runners, and add NO_PROXY: token-proxy to the runners. Test a checkout through the proxy before you roll out a class (Egress hosts). Certificate authority. Add your CA to a custom image and run update-ca-certificates, or mount a CA bundle read-only and point SSL_CERT_FILE at it. Windows images need the CA in the image. On Linux, the token proxy needs the CA too when a proxy or your CircleCI server uses it: mount the bundle into token-proxy and set SSL_CERT_FILE there (Images).
data.does-circleci-support-it#Does CircleCI s: No. See Support. Your normal CircleCI support covers the runner itself, the platform, and your resource classes. What is tested says how each claim is checked, and which are not.
data.does-it-create-or-remove-nodes#Does it c: No. You install Docker, join the node to the Swarm, and label it from a manager (a node cannot label itself), and a Windows node needs its base image before the first task. A terminated instance leaves a Down node until you run docker node rm. There is no cloud integration or machine image. If you create nodes with user data, do not leave the Swarm join token readable in it (Cloud nodes: block the metadata address). Refer to Multi-node clusters.
data.does-it-scale-to-zero-and-what-does-idle: No. Capacity is fixed and you pay for the peak: an idle replica keeps its reserved CPU and memory on nodes that you run. Scale to zero is a manual replicas: 0, and a class with no runner queues jobs without limit and holds concurrency (Capacity and concurrency). Which replica a scale-down removes is not documented, and a scale-down while jobs run is not tested: assume it can remove a busy one (on Windows it kills the job). For elastic capacity, use the machine runner orchestrator or CircleCI cloud executors.
data.does-it-support-macos#Does it support ma: No. Docker has no macOS containers, so Swarm cannot schedule macOS jobs. CircleCI documents machine runner 3 on a Mac directly, and offers hosted macOS executors.
data.does-it-work-on-hosts-without-internet-a: No, and it is not tested. Every runner needs outbound HTTPS to runner.circleci.com, and every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. A host that reaches those names through an allow list or a proxy works. On Linux the distributor download can come from your own mirror: set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL (Run the downloads from a mirror). The mirror does not replace the task agent download, and the images must come from a registry the nodes reach (Registry needs). What needs internet lists every download.
data.does-it-work-with-rootless-docker-user-n: Podman cannot run Swarm, so it cannot run this stack. Rootless Docker and userns-remap are not tested. The stack assumes a root daemon: the entrypoint checks that the runner volume belongs to root, and the secret belongs to uid 2000. Swarm also ignores userns_mode in stack files.
data.does-it-work-with-selinux-on-rhel#Does i: The RHEL steps are documented and not tested in CI. Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume, so no host directory needs a label. For a denial, refer to Troubleshooting.
data.how-do-i-report-a-bug-or-a-vulnerability: Open a GitHub issue for a bug. For a vulnerability, email security@circleci.com (SECURITY.md).
data.how-do-i-scale-up-or-down-and-see-how-ma:
Swarm has no autoscaling, so you choose the number of replicas.
Permanent. Edit deploy.replicas in your stack file and deploy again with the same files (Choose replica counts). To go beyond one node, add nodes (Multi-node clusters).
Quick. docker service scale runners_linux-default=4. The next docker stack deploy resets it. A scale-down stops containers: on Linux a running job finishes first. On Windows, scale down only while the class is idle (why).
Queue depth. Ask the runner API with a personal API token, not a resource class token:
curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=/linux-default" curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=/linux-default" The first prints {"unclaimed_task_count": 3}, the second {"running_runner_tasks": 2}. Jobs wait while unclaimed_task_count stays above 0 and every replica is busy. Raise the replicas by that number if the nodes have room (Monitor the cluster).
data.how-do-i-verify-a-release#How do I verif: Each release has a SHA256SUMS file and a keyless cosign signature made with the CircleCI OIDC token. Run the single check block on Verify a release (or on Windows): it prints RELEASE VERIFIED only when the signature, the ref (refs/heads/main) and the checksums all pass. The runner binary is a separate download: the distributor verifies its SHA-256, and on Linux the entrypoint checks it at every container start (Runner binary integrity on Linux).
data.is-docker-swarm-a-safe-bet#Is Docker Swa:
The project can state what it checks, and cannot promise the future of Swarm.
What it uses. Core Swarm features only: services, secrets, configs, overlay networks, placement constraints, rolling updates. Docker versions. CI runs Docker 29.4.2 on Linux and 29.4.0 on Windows. The documented minimum is 24 on Linux and 28.0 on Windows (Linux, Windows). The way out. Resource class names are CircleCI objects, so jobs with machine: true keep their class when you move it (alternatives). Support. Best effort, with no commitment on how long it is maintained (Support).
data.is-there-a-delay-between-jobs#Is there a: About 10 seconds for the restart delay, plus container start and the task agent download, before a replica claims the next job. Other replicas keep working meanwhile. Refer to Job lifecycle.
data.should-i-use-the-setup-helper-or-the-man:
Either. Both give the same result, and every helper step is on the install pages (Linux, Windows). A rerun is safe.
The helper does: check the node, create a single-node Swarm, create secrets from hidden prompts, and deploy the stack files you name. On Windows it also labels the node with the image tags it can run. It does not: install Docker or the runner (the distributor does), create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label or join other nodes, or build images.
data.what-do-sudo--nihu-and-setpriv-mean#What:
They are the two forms of the runner command_prefix, which makes a job run as another user (reference). The entrypoint sets it in every Linux container, and the service environment cannot override it.
sudo -niHu circleci -- is the default class: never prompt, login shell, HOME of the target user, run as circleci. /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner allows only the runner user (uid 2000), and only to the job user. setpriv (util-linux) switches to the job user and clears every capability. The hardened class always uses it with --no-new-privs, so sudo, su or a setuid binary cannot lift a job to root. An image with no sudo uses it too. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO chooses between the two classes (Users and the runner token on Linux).
data.what-happens-to-a-job-when-a-node-dies#W: The job is lost. CircleCI reports an infrastructure failure, and self-hosted runners do not retry, so rerun it. Swarm starts replacement runners on other matching nodes. A single manager that dies stops all replacements (Managers and quorum). Refer to Node death.
data.what-is-machine-runner-swarm#What is mac: It runs CircleCI machine runner 3 as Docker Swarm services: one resource class for each service, and a new container for every job. It ships stack files, a Linux entrypoint, a runner distributor service, optional setup helpers and these docs. See Concepts.
data.what-is-not-in-this-release#What is not: Autoscaling and creation of nodes. Metrics export (Monitor the cluster). An external secrets manager, and a tested rotation of tokens. A hardened Windows class, and Hyper-V isolation. CircleCI server and hosts without internet access: neither is tested (What needs internet). A one-command verification script. Use the commands of Verify a release.
data.what-is-the-token-proxy-and-what-happens:
The service token-proxy (token-proxy-windows on Windows) holds the class tokens so that runner containers and jobs never do. Runners hold a placeholder and send their API calls to the proxy, which adds the real token to the task claim, once for each container. Persistent classes do not use it. Refer to The token proxy and Security.
When it is down, no runner can claim and jobs wait in CircleCI. Idle runners fail their claims and retry, and Swarm restarts a failed proxy after 5 seconds. A running job keeps its container, but its API calls (step output) also go through the proxy, so keep outages to a restart. A claim whose outcome is unknown is latched like a successful claim: that runner is refused until Swarm replaces it, so the proxy fails closed.
Placement. The proxy runs on a manager by default. In a cluster, label its node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run there (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). Limits. Each client address gets 50 requests a second (bursts of 200), and the proxy serves at most 512 requests at once. Monitoring. Monitor the token proxy.
data.what-must-i-build#What must I build?:
Nothing, with one optional exception on Windows. Swarm pulls one published image, the token proxy (ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy), and the release bundle names it by digest.
Needs Optional Linux A Docker engine and a Swarm join. The runner-distributor service fills a per-node volume with the runner, and a stock image such as cimg/base runs it A custom image when jobs need tools (it needs util-linux setpriv). Refer to Images Windows A Docker engine, the ltsc2022 base image, and a Swarm join. The runner-distributor-windows service installs the runner and portable Git into a volume A custom image, and a DIY image that lets a job finish after a stop. Refer to Windows images and the stop-timeout image
data.where-are-the-tokens-kept-and-can-i-use-: Class tokens are Swarm secrets. There is no integration with an external secrets manager. Anyone in the docker group on a manager can read every token, and a Windows secret is stored in clear text on the disk of the proxy container (Token model on each OS). Rotation is manual and not tested in CI (Rotate a runner token).
data.which-circleci-plans-and-platforms-work#:
CircleCI cloud, on Linux and Windows. CircleCI server is not tested. To try server, change the -upstream argument of the token-proxy service to your server URL and keep CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080 on the runners (CircleCI server).
Self-hosted runners need at least one credit on your account, although runner compute does not use credits (Run jobs on self-hosted runners). Their concurrency is separate from hosted jobs and shared by every class of the organization (see the Runner tab). Config policies, which restrict classes to projects, need the Scale plan on cloud or server 4.2 or later (Config policy management overview).
data.which-jobs-cannot-run-here#Which jobs ca:
Jobs run in unprivileged containers on a shared kernel, so some belong on another runner.
Job needs Here Use instead A privileged container, /dev/kvm, or host devices No. Swarm ignores privileged and devices. The microVM add-on gives a job its own kernel, not host devices The orchestrator, or a machine runner on a host Docker-in-Docker, setup_remote_docker, or Docker commands in a job No, except in the opt-in docker-build class, which is root-equivalent on its node The docker-build class, a daemonless builder, or a daemon in the VM of the microVM add-on A GPU Not supported or tested A machine runner on a GPU host A docker: executor job, or service containers Only in container mode, a prototype, in classes of its own Container mode, or container runner Desktop or UI automation on Windows No. Windows jobs are headless A machine runner on a host
data.which-operating-systems-does-it-support#: Platform Status Linux, Ubuntu LTS, amd64 Tested in CI, including real jobs Linux, Ubuntu LTS, arm64 Every pipeline tests that the distributor installs the runner and that the stack starts. On main and smr-swarm/* branches, three probe jobs also run on a real arm64 runner Linux, ppc64le and s390x The distributor and token proxy are built for them. CI emulates them under QEMU: the distributor installs the runner of the right architecture, and the token proxy image runs. Nothing else runs there Linux, RHEL 8 and later Steps documented, not tested in CI Windows Server 2025 and 2022 Tested in CI, on amd64 Windows on arm64 The distributor is built for it. The token proxy has no windows/arm64 image (Windows). No arm64 host runs the stack in CI Windows Server 2019 Supported by machine runner 3. Untested here, and the stack files have no label for it Windows Server 2016 and older Not compatible with machine runner 3 macOS Out of scope
data.which-runner-version-do-the-nodes-run#Wh: The runner-distributor service decides. The default is an exact pin, with the tarball SHA-256 values in the stack file: the newest runner version that CI tests, bumped by each release. Nodes keep it until you change it. To float, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION to 3.1, 3 or current. Floating is weaker: the distributor trusts the manifest hash, and a newer runner can change the protocol that the proxy depends on, so the proxy fails closed and jobs wait. Pin an exact version in production. runner-distributor-windows works the same way. Refer to The version policy and Upgrade the runner on Windows.
data.why-does-a-windows-job-end-when-i-update: Stopping a busy Windows container kills its job after about 5 seconds, whatever stop_grace_period says. Change a class only while it is idle, or rerun the interrupted jobs (why).
data.why-not-plain-docker-compose#Why not pla:
Compose restarts the same container, so files outside the working directory survive into the next job. Swarm creates a new task and container for every job, keeps the token in a Swarm secret instead of an environment file visible in docker inspect, and adds many nodes with placement, rolling updates and drain. The price is Swarm concepts, even on one node.
linux/tests/ephemerality.sh has a negative control: three jobs on docker run --restart always ran in one container, and two found files from an earlier job. To move off the old docker-compose.yml, refer to Migrate from Docker Compose.
data.why-swarm-and-not-container-runner-or-an:
Choose by what you already run and the isolation you need.
You have or need Use Elastic capacity, nothing to host CircleCI cloud executors Kubernetes, jobs that fit a docker: executor Container runner A boundary stronger than a container, privileged or KVM jobs, a full OS, autoscaling Machine runner orchestrator: a VM for each job on Kubernetes with KubeVirt, and the token stays out of the VM (comparison) One host or a few, jobs that need the whole machine Machine runner 3 on a host: the simplest setup, nothing separates one job from the next The same, in a container Machine runner 3 on Docker: the container is reused, so the environment is not clean Docker hosts or Windows containers, no Kubernetes, a clean container for every job Machine runner swarm: replicas, placement, secrets and rolling updates. No CircleCI support, no autoscaling, no node creation, and containers share the host kernel The stack files use only core Swarm features. To move to the orchestrator or a plain machine runner later, keep the resource class names, and jobs with machine: true stay as they are. Container runner needs jobs that use a docker: executor.
The microVM add-on runs each job in a Kata Containers microVM on Swarm nodes with KVM. It is experimental: CI runs the real runner against a fake CircleCI API on nested virtualization on AWS (amd64), and no real CircleCI job, other cloud, or arm64 is tested in CI. One real CircleCI job ran by hand on a Kata Cloud Hypervisor class. If you need a hardware boundary today, use the orchestrator.

data: Quickstart on Linux: Run a first job with CircleCI machine runner 3 on one Docker Swarm node in five steps. A trial: the node cannot join a cluster later. Quickstart on Windows Server: Run a first job on a Windows Server Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in five steps, using the stock Server Core image. Concepts: How Swarm services map to resource classes, what the token proxy does, what a clean environment covers, and how the default and hardened classes differ.

Machine runner swarm runs CircleCI machine runner 3 as Docker Swarm services. Swarm handles replicas, restarts, secrets, and placement. Read this page before you change a stack file or choose between the default and the hardened class.
data.add-on-stack-files-and-how-they-merge#Ad:
Each operating system has one main stack file, runners.yaml, that defines the default classes and deploys on its own. Optional classes live in add-on stack files next to it:
File System Adds classes-extra.yaml Linux linux-java and the hardened linux-hardened persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml Linux and Windows Persistent, Docker-build and SSH-rerun classes custom-image.yaml Windows A class with your own image microvm.yaml Linux MicroVM classes (MicroVM jobs) container-mode.yaml Linux The prototype container agent for Docker-executor jobs (Container mode) An add-on stack file is not a patch of the main file. It defines services of its own, and each service needs its own resource class and -token secret. On Linux, classes-extra.yaml, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml, and microvm.yaml also add their classes to the token-proxy service, so deploy them together with runners.yaml. persistent.yaml and container-mode.yaml keep their own tokens and do not touch the proxy.
docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml runners merges the files in the order given, as Docker Compose does for several -f files. A service, network, secret, or volume that only one file defines is added, and a key that several files set takes the value of the later file. YAML anchors work inside one file only, so each add-on stack file repeats the common service settings.
Pass the same files, in the same order, on every deploy: the services of a file you leave out stay as they are and stop following your edits, and --prune removes them. Check a merge without a Swarm with docker stack config -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml.
data.glossary#Glossary: Term Meaning Stack file A Compose-format YAML file that docker stack deploy reads: a main file (runners.yaml) for each OS and optional add-on stack files. An add-on stack file is not a Docker overlay network Stack The services that one docker stack deploy creates, named runners here, so the service linux-default is runners_linux-default in Swarm commands Resource class, service A resource class is the CircleCI name, /, that a job selects with resource_class. A service is the Swarm object that runs it, named like the class without the namespace runner-bin, current, record runner-bin is the named volume, one on every node, that holds the runner versions under versions/. current is the link to the active version, which a container resolves once at start. The record is versions//SHA256, the SHA-256 of the binary in sha256sum -c format, which the entrypoint checks at every container start Runner distributor The global service runner-distributor (Linux) or runner-distributor-windows (it installs portable Git too) that downloads, verifies, and installs the runner into runner-bin, moves current, and looks again every MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL Drain A runner drain happens when the runner gets SIGTERM: it takes no new job and finishes the running one. A node drain is docker node update --availability drain: Swarm stops the tasks of that node, which starts a runner drain in each, and starts replacements on other nodes.
data.job-lifecycle#Job lifecycle:
Swarm never reuses a container. Every exit (a finished job, an idle timeout, a crash) leads to a new task and a new container, because the restart policy is condition: any.
sequenceDiagram participant S as Swarm participant C as Container participant A as runner.circleci.com participant N as New container S->>C: start a task from the image C->>A: poll for a job (single-task mode) A-->>C: claim one job C->>C: run the job in a clean container C-->>S: runner exits, container stops Note over S: restart_policy any, delay 10s S->>N: create a NEW task and container N->>A: poll for the next jobOn Linux the entrypoint checks the runner, sets up the users, and starts it, and the runner steps the job down to the job user. On Windows the runner is the main process. Timing:
A replica needs about 10 seconds (the restart delay) plus container start-up before it can claim the next job. The other replicas keep claiming in the meantime. Every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. Allow this host in your egress rules. A single-task runner that finds no job exits after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT (1h in the stack files), so idle replicas pick up a rotated secret or a new image within an hour. Stopping a service sends SIGTERM to the runner. The runner drains: it accepts no new job and lets the running job finish. The stack sets stop_grace_period: 5h5m, the runner max_run_time of 5 hours plus 5 minutes.
On Windows, change a class only while it is idle (why).
data.placement-labels#Placement labels: Services carry constraints and nodes advertise capabilities. The built-in properties are node.platform.os and node.platform.arch. Machine runner swarm adds the node labels machine-runner-swarm.zone, machine-runner-swarm.proxy, machine-runner-swarm.docker-build, machine-runner-swarm.container-mode, machine-runner-swarm.microvm, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025, and machine-runner-swarm.class.. See Multi-node clusters.
data.services-are-resource-classes#Services a:
Each Swarm service is one CircleCI resource class. The service name is the short name of the class, so the service linux-default serves the resource class /linux-default. A job selects the class in its config:
jobs: build: machine: true resource_class: /linux-default Each service also has one Swarm secret, -token, which holds the token of that class. In the single-task classes the token proxy holds it, and the runners hold a placeholder. A persistent class mounts its token in the runner container itself.
flowchart TB nodes["Nodes: Linux amd64, Linux arm64, WindowsLabels decide where tasks may run"] subgraph services["Swarm services: one for each resource class"] direction LR s1["linux-defaultreplicas: 2"] s2["linux-pythonreplicas: 1"] s3["windows-defaultreplicas: 2"] end r1["container 1"] r2["container 2"] r3["container 1"] r4["container 1"] r5["container 2"] api["runner.circleci.comOutbound HTTPS 443 only, through the token proxy for single-task classes"] nodes --> services s1 --> r1 & r2 s2 --> r3 s3 --> r4 & r5 r1 & r2 & r3 & r4 & r5 --> apiThe runner containers poll CircleCI for work, through the token proxy in the single-task classes. Nothing connects to a runner, so the main stack files publish no ports.
deploy.replicas is the number of runners in the class, and so the number of jobs it runs at the same time. A replica that fits on no node stays Pending until capacity is free. Resource classes covers sizing.
data.single-task-or-continuous-mode#Single-ta:
The stack files set the runner mode with CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE.
Mode Value Behavior Environment Single-task single-task (default in every stack file) The runner claims one job, runs it, and exits. Swarm starts a new container for the next job Clean for every job Continuous continuous (persistent classes only) The runner stays up and claims job after job in the same container Shared by all jobs on that runner Use continuous mode only for trusted projects that need warm caches: Persistent mode.
data.the-runner-distributor-on-linux#The runn:
The Linux services use stock images such as cimg/base, and the image holds none of the runner. The service runner-distributor puts the runner on every Linux node that runs the classes of runners.yaml. docker stack deploy is the only upgrade path.
The service. runner-distributor is a global service from the stock alpine:3 image (pinned by digest), so it runs on every Linux node, also a Docker-build node and a node that joins later. A microVM node (machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true) is the exception: the microVM classes download their own runner into each VM (MicroVM jobs). Its script, linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh, is a Swarm config. The volume. It writes to runner-bin, one named volume on every node. Each version has a directory versions/ with bin/circleci-runner, SHA256, VERSION, and TARBALL. The link current points to the active version and moves with one atomic rename. The file history lists the versions in the order they were active. The runner services. Every class mounts runner-bin read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The entrypoint is another Swarm config, mounted at /circleci-runner-entrypoint with the mode 0555. A job cannot change either. The wait. The entrypoint waits up to MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT seconds (default 120) until current exists, so a first deploy and a new node need no order. Without a runner, or with a binary that differs from its record, it exits with code 80, and Swarm retries after the restart delay. A container resolves current once, so a running job keeps its version and the next container gets the new one. A persistent class runs one container for all jobs, so it picks up a new version when its container restarts (Recycle a class). The runner services carry no version and no hash: the version is a setting of the distributor service only, so an upgrade, a pin, and a rollback change that one service, and the runner services never restart. An idle replica keeps the old binary until it recycles, within the idle timeout of 1 hour.
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION Behavior 3.1.13 (an exact version, the default: the newest that CI tests) A pin. The tarball is checked against the SHA-256 values that the stack file carries for it, not the manifest. It never changes by itself, makes no request once installed, and switches to an installed version without network, so a rollback needs no download. A release bumps the version and its SHA-256 values together 3.1 or 3 A floating line: the newest 3.1.x, or the newest 3.x.y, of CircleCI’s manifest. Checked again every 24 hours. It ignores the default SHA-256 list and trusts the hash of the manifest, which is weaker current CircleCI’s current release, within major version 3. Checked again every 24 hours, and trusts the manifest hash like the floating lines See The version policy for the rules, Upgrade the runner on Linux for the settings, and Runner binary integrity on Linux for the checks.
data.the-runner-distributor-on-windows#The ru:
The Windows services use the stock Server Core image, with none of the runner and none of Git. The service runner-distributor-windows does what the Linux distributor does, with the same settings and version policy.
The service. A global service on the nodes with the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, from the stock servercore:ltsc2022 image with process isolation. Its script, windows\stack\runner-distributor.ps1, is a Swarm config. The volume and the links. It writes to runner-bin: versions\ for the runner (with SHA256, TARBALL and VERSION), git\ for portable Git, and two relative directory symbolic links, current and git\current. Every class mounts the volume read-only twice, with volume.subpath: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe. No entrypoint. circleci-runner.exe is the main process. A runner task that starts before the first flip fails and starts again after the restart delay, so a new node needs no order. Nothing checks the binary when a container starts: Runner binary integrity on Windows. Locked files. Windows cannot replace or delete files that a running container uses. The distributor installs a version next to the others, flips the link, and removes an old version only when no container uses it. No busy job is killed by an upgrade. See Upgrade the runner on Windows for the settings.
data.the-token-proxy#The token proxy:
The service token-proxy of runners.yaml (on Windows token-proxy-windows, which works the same way, with the differences in Windows) keeps the class tokens away from the runners and their jobs. A runner sends its API calls to the proxy (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080) and holds only a placeholder token. The proxy adds the class token to one call, the task claim, and passes every other call on to CircleCI. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response for the rest.
flowchart LR subgraph cls["Class overlay networks"] r1["linux-default runnersplaceholder token"] r2["linux-python runnersplaceholder token"] end p["token-proxyone replicaholds every class token"] api["runner.circleci.com"] r1 -- "claim, task calls" --> p r2 -- "claim, task calls" --> p p -- "HTTPS: the class token on the claim only" --> apiThe network decides who may claim, not what a runner says. The proxy allows a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks. of a class, once for each container. A container that is not a runner, or a runner that claims a second time, gets 403. A claim whose outcome is unknown counts as a claim, so the proxy fails closed. The token proxy lists what it protects and what it does not, and Monitor the token proxy covers what happens when it is down.
What the proxy changes for you:
Secrets. You create the class secrets -token, and one more, runner-placeholder-token, with a dummy token. Only the proxy mounts the class secrets. Every runner mounts the placeholder. Classes. A new single-task class needs two lines in the proxy: its network (Linux) and its secret -token. See Resource classes. The persistent classes do not use the proxy. The image. ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (the signature is the trust root, not the name): a static Go binary on a minimal base, with no shell. One tag covers Linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, and Windows Server 2022 and 2025 (amd64). Swarm pulls it, and every digest is signed: The token proxy image, Verify the token proxy image. The state. The proxy keeps the addresses of the runners that have claimed in the volume proxy-state, on the node that it runs on (a manager by default). If it moves, the state stays behind: Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. In a cluster, label the node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so jobs do not share a node with the proxy. On a single node, set no label.
data.users-and-the-runner-token-on-linux#User:
Inside each Linux container, two accounts exist:
The runner user circleci-runner (uid 2000) runs circleci-runner and owns the token file. It has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The job user runs every job step. It is circleci in the cimg images, or the account you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER. The runner steps each job down to the job user with command_prefix: sudo -niHu -- in the default class, setpriv when the image has no sudo, and always setpriv --no-new-privs in the hardened class. The token is never in the job environment, and the config file that the runner reads is readable only by the runner user and root. In the single-task classes that file holds the placeholder.
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO decides the rest:
Class type Setting Jobs have sudo Can a job read the class token Default (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) "true" Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No, the container holds a placeholder. Only a job that escapes onto the node of the proxy can Hardened (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) "false" No No, for the same reason Persistent (linux-persistent, no proxy) "false" (the shipped file; "true" is the opt-in) No (with "true": yes) No, as in the hardened class. With "true", yes if the job uses sudo (The persistent class) The default class. Jobs keep the passwordless sudo that many orgs and orbs expect, for example sudo apt-get install. A job that uses sudo is root in its container: it can read the placeholder and the files of the runner, and become the runner user, but it finds no class token (linux/tests/proxy.sh scans the containers as root to show it).
The hardened class. The entrypoint steps every job down with util-linux setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and edits no file of the image. Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so setuid binaries such as sudo and su stay in the image. The kernel flag that setpriv sets is inherited by the job and everything it starts, and cannot be cleared, so no setuid binary can lift a job to root, even through a local-root bug.
The container exits with code 80 if the image has no util-linux setpriv. Jobs cannot install system packages at run time, and nothing in a job gains privileges through setuid or file capabilities (for example ping or mount). Build the tools into the image. CircleCI also recommends pre-installing dependencies as the most secure option. A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root, because the containers share the host kernel. Choose the hardened class for shared or regulated work, and the default class for a single trusted team that needs sudo. See Security.
data.users-and-the-runner-token-on-windows#Us:
Windows containers have no step-down: the runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs its symbolic link privilege to install the task agent. A job can read the config file of its runner. In a single-task class it holds only the placeholder (the class token is in token-proxy-windows), in the persistent class the real token. The token is not in the job environment. A hostile job on the same host as the proxy can still reach it, because process isolation is not a security boundary (Windows).
Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary: one token for each class, restricted users, rotated tokens. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER do not exist on Windows. See Token model on each OS.
data.what-a-clean-environment-covers#What a c:
A clean environment means that a job starts in a container created from the image, with nothing left by an earlier job.
Covered Not covered Files and installed packages anywhere in the container filesystem Anything on a mounted volume: persistent classes keep a named volume by design The home directory, /tmp, and the working directory The Docker engine of the node when a class mounts its socket or named pipe: images, containers, and build cache persist Processes, environment variables, and shell history State outside the node, such as databases, registries, and shared storage Users, groups, and sudo rules created by an earlier job The kernel: all containers on a node share it On Windows, the registry, the user profile, %TEMP%, and C:\ProgramData Data of finished containers that Swarm has not yet pruned from the node disk The runner is mounted read-only, so a job cannot change what the next job runs (The runner distributor on Linux, The runner distributor on Windows). A single-task class needs no working directory cleanup, because the container is discarded. On Linux the runner does not clean it, because the runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns: the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false" (Working directory cleanup).
Containers are not a virtual machine boundary. Read Security before you run untrusted code.
data.what-the-linux-entrypoint-does#What the:
circleci-runner-entrypoint starts as root, prepares the container, and runs the runner as the runner user. It never reads the token or the placeholder. In order, it:
Waits for the runner distributor, resolves current once, and checks the binary against its SHA-256 record. It also checks that the runner and every directory above it, up to /opt/machine-runner-swarm, are owned by root and not writable by the group or others. Looks for the tools it needs: sudo or util-linux setpriv to step jobs down, and setpriv or su to start the runner. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs is required. Without the tools it exits with code 80 (What an image needs). Creates the users with useradd or adduser (sudo refuses a user that has no passwd and no shadow entry): circleci-runner with uid and gid 2000, and the job user when the image has none. Sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX. A value in the service environment does not override it. With sudo, the prefix is ["sudo","-niHu","","--"]. The file /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner lets uid 2000 run commands as the job user only, and keeps the PATH and environment variables of the image. Without sudo, or with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, it is a setpriv command that gives the job no capabilities (in the hardened class also --no-new-privs), run through env -u for every CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variable of the container (the runner name stays). The runner holds CAP_SETUID and CAP_SETGID as ambient capabilities only to call it. Creates the task agent and working directories, adds the job user to the group of /var/run/docker.sock when the class mounts the socket (Docker builds), and runs the runner with exec as uid 2000. The init process (init: true) passes SIGTERM to it, which starts the runner drain. It does not validate the runner name, the token, the mode, or the timeouts: the runner checks its own settings and exits with code 80 for a bad one. With sudo, a job gets the environment variables of the image (PATH, JAVA_HOME, LANG), the variables you set in the service (such as a proxy), and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME, and nothing else from the runner.
data.why-swarm-and-not-plain-compose#Why Swar: A plain docker compose up restarts the same container, so the environment is not clean. Swarm creates a new container for every task. The FAQ lists the trade-offs.

data:
Go from nothing to a first job on one Linux node in five steps. The page sets up one class, linux-default, and installs nothing on the node by hand: a service of the stack installs the runner.
Note CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, not supported by CircleCI support. This trial runs on one node, so it has no high availability. What is tested shows what CI checks.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: A node with Ubuntu LTS, Docker Engine 24 or later, curl, a clock synced with NTP, and outbound HTTPS (what needs internet). Prepare each node shows how to install Docker. Size: 6 CPUs and 10 GB for the two sample replicas. A smaller node can run one replica (step 4). The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, on your workstation. An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms. A repository that is set up as a CircleCI project in your organization, and runner concurrency in your plan (2 for the sample replicas). A namespace. An organization has one, and orbs use it too. It is the part before the / in a resource class (acme in acme/my-class). If you have none, run circleci namespace create --org . Replace with your namespace, and with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID. Run step 1 on your workstation, where a browser opens for circleci auth login. Run steps 2 to 4 on the node. They use sudo, because the docker group is equivalent to root.
data.next#Next: Install on Linux: every step by hand, RHEL, release verification, and upgrades. Before production, copy linux/stack to a directory of your own and deploy that copy (Review the stack file). Concepts: services as resource classes, the token proxy, and the job lifecycle. Resource classes: add classes, and change sizes and replicas. Security: choose the default or the hardened class before you give a class to a team. Operations: pin or roll back the runner, rotate tokens, and run the cluster. Uninstall: remove the trial, and leave the swarm. Troubleshooting: symptoms, causes, and fixes.
data.steps#Steps:
Create a resource class and a token. Copy the token from the output: the command prints it once, and step 3 asks for it on the node.
circleci auth login circleci runner resource-class create /linux-default --org --generate-token On the node, download the latest release. To verify the release signature first, see Install on Linux: Verify a release.
version=$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest) version=${version##*/v} curl -fsSL "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v${version}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" | tar -xz cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}" Swarm takes 10.0.0.0/8 for its overlay networks. If your network uses that range, run docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 --listen-addr 127.0.0.1:2377 --default-addr-pool --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24 yourself, and run the next command without --swarm-init. Otherwise, the next command starts a one-node Swarm that listens on the loopback address:
sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init No other node can join this Swarm: a cluster later needs a new swarm init and new secrets. The runners share the node with the token proxy, so a job that escapes its container could read the class tokens. Use it for a trial. For a cluster, follow Multi-node clusters instead.
Create the secrets. The first command asks for the token from step 1 (hidden input). The token goes to the token proxy only. The second creates the placeholder that the runners read instead of a token.
sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder Deploy the stack, and check it. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a minute to start.
sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy sudo docker stack services runners circleci runner instance list --org --resource-class /linux-default The stack is up when runners_linux-default shows 2/2, runners_token-proxy shows 1/1, and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. The stack reserves 4.1 CPUs and a little over 8 GB, plus what the system needs. If a replica stays Pending, the node is too small. Run one replica:
sudo docker service scale runners_linux-default=1 The next docker stack deploy resets it to 2. To keep one, set deploy.replicas in your copy of the stack file (Size the limits, A task stays pending).
Run a job. Save this as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace with your namespace, then commit and push. The same file is examples/linux-hello.yml.
version: 2.1 jobs: hello: machine: true resource_class: /linux-default steps: - run: name: Show where this job runs command: | echo "runner: $CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME" if [ -e /tmp/hello-marker ]; then echo "the container was reused"; exit 1; fi touch /tmp/hello-marker echo "clean container: no marker from an earlier job" workflows: hello: jobs: - hello Run the workflow twice. Both runs pass, because Swarm starts a new container for each job. The job shows Queued while no runner is online: check step 4 first.

data:
Go from nothing to a first job on one Windows Server node in five steps. Nothing is built or installed on the host: the stack uses the stock Server Core image, and a service of the stack installs the runner and Git.
Note CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, not supported by CircleCI support. This trial runs the proxy and the jobs on one host, so it is not for production. What is tested shows what CI checks.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: A Windows Server 2022 or 2025 host (amd64, not a domain controller) with a clock synced with NTP, and outbound HTTPS (what needs internet). Size: 6 CPUs and 12 GB for the two sample replicas, or run one replica (4 CPUs, 8 GB). The first pull of the Server Core image is about 2.2 GB. Docker Engine and CLI 28.0 or later in Windows-container mode, and the Windows Containers feature. Check with docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}' and docker info --format '{{.OSType}}' (it must print windows). If either fails, follow Prerequisites. The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, on your workstation. An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms. A repository that is set up as a CircleCI project in your organization, and runner concurrency in your plan (2 for the sample replicas). A namespace. An organization has one, and orbs use it too. It is the part before the / in a resource class (acme in acme/my-class). If you have none, run circleci namespace create --org . An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session on the host. Replace with your namespace, and with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID. Run step 1 on your workstation, where a browser opens for circleci auth login. Run steps 2 to 4 in the PowerShell session on the host.
data.next#Next: Install on Windows Server: every step by hand, release verification, and upgrades. Before production, copy windows\stack to a directory of your own and deploy that copy (Review the stack files). Concepts: services as resource classes, the token proxy, and the job lifecycle. Images: add your own tools on top of Server Core. Security: the token model and BitLocker. Operations: upgrade, rotate tokens, and run the cluster. Uninstall: remove the trial, and leave the swarm.
data.steps#Steps:
Create a resource class and a token. Copy the token from the output: the command prints it once, and step 3 asks for it on the host.
circleci auth login circleci runner resource-class create <NAMESPACE>/windows-default --org <ORG> --generate-token On the host, download the latest release. To verify the release signature first, see Install on Windows Server: Verify a release.
$uri = (Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri 'https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest').BaseResponse.ResponseUri.AbsoluteUri $version = $uri -replace '^.*/v', '' $zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip" Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v$version/$zip" -OutFile $zip Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath . cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version" Pull the images, then run the helper. Pull first: the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init. The first command pulls the base image, and the second pulls the token proxy image that your stack file names.
docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 docker pull ((Select-String -Path windows\stack\runners.yaml -Pattern 'MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE:-([^}]+)\}').Matches[0].Groups[1].Value) The helper needs the IPv4 address of the host. If the host has several, use the address of the adapter that other nodes will reach. For a one-host trial, any address of the host works.
Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 -PrefixOrigin Dhcp,Manual | Select-Object IPAddress, InterfaceAlias Swarm takes 10.0.0.0/8 for its overlay networks. If your network uses that range, run docker swarm init --advertise-addr --default-addr-pool --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24 yourself, and run the helper below without -InitSwarm and -AdvertiseAddr. Otherwise, the helper creates the Swarm, labels the node, asks for the token from step 1 (hidden input), creates the secrets, and deploys the stack:
.\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr <HOST_IPV4_ADDRESS> -Class windows-default -Deploy Check the stack. docker stack deploy does not wait, and the first start downloads the runner, so the replicas need a few minutes. Early runner tasks fail until the download ends, and Swarm restarts them.
docker stack services runners circleci runner instance list --org <ORG> --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/windows-default The stack is up when runners_windows-default shows 2/2, runners_token-proxy-windows shows 1/1, and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows shows the install. If a replica stays Pending, the host is too small: each replica reserves 2 CPUs and 4 GB, and the proxy and the distributor reserve nothing but can use 1 CPU each. The Windows engine rejects a CPU limit above the CPU count of the host. Run one replica:
docker service scale runners_windows-default=1 The next docker stack deploy resets it to 2. To keep one, set deploy.replicas in your copy of the stack file (Size the limits, A task stays pending).
Run a job. Save this as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace with your namespace, then commit and push. The file examples/windows-job.yml has more steps.
version: 2.1 jobs: hello: machine: true resource_class: /windows-default steps: - run: echo "computer $COMPUTERNAME, instance $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID" workflows: hello: jobs: - hello Run the workflow twice. The two runs print different values, because Swarm starts a new container for each job. The job shows Queued while no runner is online: check step 4 first. The default shell is Git Bash, so $COMPUTERNAME is an environment variable. For PowerShell, set shell: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass and write $env:COMPUTERNAME.
data.what-differs-from-linux#What differs fro: A job runs as an administrator. The runner container holds a placeholder, and the class token stays in the token proxy, except in the windows-persistent class (Token model on each OS). Stopping a busy container, for an update, a scale-down or a drain, kills its job after about 5 seconds. Change a class while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

data: Linux: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Ubuntu or RHEL, with one clean container for every job. Windows Server: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server 2022 or 2025, with one clean container for every job. Multi-node clusters: Join Linux, Windows, and Arm nodes to one Docker Swarm, place resource classes with labels and constraints, and open the ports that the nodes need.

This page deploys CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Linux: one service for each resource class, and a clean container for every job. The steps cover one node (Multi-node clusters adds more). For a first run, Quickstart on Linux is shorter.
Note Tested against CircleCI cloud only (What is tested). Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add nodes or scale to the queue. On Kubernetes, use container runner.
A service of the stack installs the runner on every node. The optional setup helper runs the same steps.
data.1-create-the-resource-classes#1. Create:
Create a namespace if your organization has none. An organization has one namespace, and orbs use the same one.
circleci namespace create --org Create one resource class for each service in the stack file. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml has one service, linux-default: keep that name for a first run.
circleci runner resource-class create /linux-default --org --generate-token The command prints a token once: store it in your secret manager. If you lose it, run circleci runner token create / --nickname . To rename the service, edit your copy of the file first (step 5), then create the class and the secret under the new name. More classes: Resource classes.
data.2-prepare-each-node#2. Prepare each node: Run these steps on every node that runs services. A single node needs no firewall change. Multi-node clusters open the ports in Inter-node ports.
data.3-start-swarm#3. Start Swarm:
Run every docker command in these steps with sudo, or as a user in the docker group. On a single node, start Swarm on the loopback address only, so nothing is exposed to the network.
docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 --listen-addr 127.0.0.1:2377 docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 The second command keeps fewer stopped containers on the node (each finished job leaves one until Swarm prunes its task). setup.sh --swarm-init runs both.
The node is a manager, and the token proxy runs on a manager by default. On a single node, set no proxy label. In a cluster, label the node that runs the proxy: runner services never run on a node with this label, so a job never shares a node with the proxy.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true With several managers, also pin the proxy to one (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). A loopback node cannot accept other nodes: for a cluster, use a routable address (Multi-node clusters).
data.4-create-the-secrets#4. Create the secre:
Create one secret for each service in the stack file, named -token. It is a runner config file that holds only the token:
api: auth_token: The token proxy mounts these secrets at /run/secrets/-token (uid 65534, mode 0400), and the runners never see them. The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a dummy token in the same format, mounted at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml (runner user, uid 2000, mode 0400). Only the persistent class mounts its own token in the runner. Every other runner setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable in the stack file.
Set classes to every class you deploy. The loop asks for each token with a hidden prompt, so the token does not reach your shell history or the process list. It works in bash, zsh and dash and stops at an empty token. Do not use read -rsp: zsh reads -p as a coprocess, which leaves TOKEN empty and creates a secret without a token.
classes="linux-default" for class in $classes; do printf 'Token for %s (hidden): ' "$class" stty -echo; IFS= read -r TOKEN; stty echo; echo [ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "no token entered for $class" >&2; break; } printf 'api:
 auth_token: %s
' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create "$class-token" - done unset TOKEN printf 'api:
 auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder
' | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token - docker stack deploy fails with secret not found when a service references a missing secret: create every secret the file references, or delete the services you do not need from your copy. docker stack config prints the mode 0400 as 256.
data.5-review-the-stack-file#5. Review the st:
Copy linux/stack to a directory of your own, deploy/, and keep it under version control. From here on you check and deploy your copy and never the shipped files. For a first run, change nothing.
cp -r linux/stack deploy Check that the file parses. This needs no running Swarm.
docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null The directory holds the stack files and the two scripts that they ship as Swarm configs, circleci-runner-entrypoint and runner-distributor.sh. Keep the scripts next to the stack files, and keep the service runner-distributor and the top-level configs: and volumes:. A Swarm config cannot change, so its name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file: if you edit a script, rename its config the same way (sha256sum | cut -c1-12).
Review these settings first (Resource classes has the details):
Setting Default Change it to Service name linux-default Your resource class name image cimg/base:2026.10 Your image, pinned by digest (Images) deploy.replicas 2 The number of concurrent jobs you need deploy.resources 2 CPUs and 4 GB The size of one runner. Limits and reservations are equal placement.constraints node.platform.os == linux Add architecture or zone constraints x-distributor-env An exact runner version (3.1.13 in this release) with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, major version 3, a check every 24 hours Nothing for a first run. A newer pin, a floating version or a mirror are variables of docker stack deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux) The optional classes are add-on files in deploy/. Add each with another -c flag, and pass the same list on every deploy (how the files merge). Each needs its own resource class and secret -token.
File Services Purpose classes-extra.yaml linux-java, linux-hardened Examples: an image swap, and a class without sudo. Reserves 6 more CPUs and 12 GB (Define a class) docker-build.yaml linux-docker-build Builds images with the host engine. Needs a labeled worker (Docker builds) microvm.yaml linux-microvm, linux-microvm-docker, microvm-dns Each job in a Kata Containers microVM. Needs KVM (MicroVM jobs) persistent.yaml linux-persistent A long-lived runner. Needs the node name edited in the file (Persistent mode) ssh-rerun.yaml linux-default-ssh Rerun job with SSH. Publishes port 54782 (Rerun job with SSH) An add-on file repeats the common settings of runners.yaml (YAML anchors do not cross files), so it also loads alone. Change a common setting, such as stop_grace_period or the logging options, in every file that you use.
data.6-deploy-the-stack#6. Deploy the stack:
Deploy your copy from step 5. The command returns before the replicas run, because docker stack deploy does not wait.
docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners To add optional classes, pass your copies with more -c flags, and pass the same list on every later deploy:
docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners The runner-distributor service starts on every Linux node, also on a node that joins later (not on a microVM node: its classes download their own runner). It downloads the pinned runner, checks its SHA-256 and puts it in the runner-bin volume. A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for it. The service token-proxy pulls its image from Docker Hub.
Other distributor settings, such as a floating version like 3.1 (weaker: the distributor trusts the manifest and ignores the default SHA-256 list), are variables of this command. sudo drops the environment: write sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 docker stack deploy ... (Upgrade the runner on Linux).
data.get-the-files#Get the files:
Use a release (recommended) or clone the repository at a release tag. Paths on this page are relative to the root of the repository or of the extracted bundle.
git clone --branch https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm.git cd machine-runner-swarm Use a release: its stack files pin the token proxy image by tag and digest. A clone uses latest, which is not a pin (The token proxy image). Each GitHub release carries four files, with the release number without the v:
File Content machine-runner-swarm-.tar.gz The Linux bundle: stack files, scripts, documentation and examples, without the tests, plus VERSION and CHANGELOG.md machine-runner-swarm-.zip The same bundle for Windows SHA256SUMS The SHA-256 checksum of both bundles SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json A keyless cosign signature of SHA256SUMS To verify the signature first, see Verify a release.
data.next#Next: Uninstall Troubleshooting: the most common problems on a first install are a missing secret, a node whose distributor cannot download the runner, and a task that stays pending because no node matches its constraints Concepts Resource classes Security Operations Machine runner 3 configuration reference
data.optional-use-the-setup-helper#Optional::
linux/setup.sh runs the steps above with checks. It never prints the token, every step is idempotent, and it needs bash 4.4 or later. It installs nothing on a node: the service runner-distributor installs the runner.
Step Effect --check Preflight: Linux on amd64, arm64, ppc64le or s390x, Docker running and 24 or later, Swarm state, NTP --swarm-init Runs docker swarm init on the loopback address unless Swarm is active, and sets the task history limit to 2 --secret Creates the secret -token from a token read on stdin --deploy Runs docker stack deploy with each --stack-file. Without one it deploys the shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml, so pass your copy from step 5. It warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest With no step it runs --check. Steps run in the order of the table. Options are --stack-file (repeatable) and --stack-name. Each run ends with Next: and the steps still to do, or Check: and the commands that show the runners start.
sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml --secret asks for the token with a hidden prompt. To script it, pipe the token (printf %s "$TOKEN" | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default). Several --secret values need a terminal. A token has only letters, digits, ., _ and -, and an existing secret stays unchanged (Rotate a runner token). Create a secret for every service you deploy. The helper does not label nodes. For a docker-build class, run docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true . The distributor reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 from the environment of --deploy, and the token proxy reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_*. sudo drops the environment: use sudo env VAR=value linux/setup.sh --deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux).
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known. The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. Pass --org (a slug such as gh/my-org, or a UUID): without it the CLI uses the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours. Docker Engine 24 or later, running, with Swarm mode (Podman cannot run Swarm). Root access or membership of the docker group, which is equivalent to root: limit it to administrators. A node clock synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts. Outbound HTTPS from each node to the hosts in Egress hosts: the release bucket of CircleCI (the runner), and the registries of the alpine image (the distributor) and the token proxy image (Docker Hub). No inbound access is needed. What needs internet lists everything. Hosts without internet access are not tested (mirrors). CPU and memory: the shipped file reserves 4.1 CPUs and a little over 8 GB (two runners and the token proxy). Replicas that do not fit stay pending (Size the limits). Runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan for your replicas (Capacity and concurrency). Operating system Architecture Status Ubuntu LTS amd64, arm64 Tested in CI on Ubuntu 26.04. On arm64, every pipeline checks that the stack installs the runner and starts, and probe jobs run on a real arm64 runner on main and smr-swarm/* branches RHEL 8 and later, and compatible distributions amd64, arm64 Steps documented, not tested in CI Any of the above ppc64le, s390x CI only starts the distributor and the token proxy image under emulation: no job has run on them
data.rhel#RHEL: Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository: Install Docker Engine on RHEL. The Podman packages of RHEL cannot run Swarm. Do steps 2 and 3 of Ubuntu. Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume, so no host directory needs a label. Note CI does not run on RHEL, so these steps follow Docker’s documentation and have not been exercised.
data.self-hosted-runner-terms-agreement#Self-: An organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms before you install self-hosted runners through the web app. Through the CLI, you agree by installing and using them (details). Whether the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered is for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy is the one container that holds your class tokens (The token proxy). It is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs), which the stack file pulls on deploy. The name is not the trust root: the signature check of Verify the token proxy image is. It is a static Go binary that runs as a non-root user with a read-only root file system, and one tag covers linux/amd64, linux/arm64, linux/ppc64le and linux/s390x. Windows nodes get the Windows image from the same tag (Windows).
Tag What it is X.Y.Z The image of a release. It never changes: pin this one X.Y, X The newest release of that minor or major line latest The newest release. The default of the stack files in a checkout, and only a release moves it edge The newest commit of the main branch that passed the end-to-end tests. For testing main, not for jobs that matter sha-<12 characters> One commit of the main branch, published before its tests have run The stack file reads the image from MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE. A release bundle defaults to ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:@sha256:, a checkout to ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest (linux/setup.sh --deploy warns when the variable is not pinned by digest). To use another image (a digest for a pin, a registry of your own for an air gap, a local build for development), set the variable in the environment of docker stack deploy. The image must be on the node that runs the proxy, so build a local one there, or copy it with docker save.
docker build -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev proxy/ sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Upgrade the token proxy says how to change its tag.
data.ubuntu#Ubuntu:
Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository: Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu.
Start the engine and confirm it runs.
sudo systemctl enable --now docker docker version Confirm the clock is synchronized. The command prints yes.
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
data.upgrade#Upgrade:
The nodes keep the runner version that the stack file pins until you change it: Upgrade the runner and images covers versions, images and rollback.
A new release changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy/ is not updated by itself. To merge:
Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.
Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old directory is the base of the merge (for a cloned tag, use git worktree or a second clone).
Set the two versions, and see what changed between the releases.
old= new= diff -ru "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack" "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack" Merge each file that differs into your copy. The command edits the file in place, marks conflicts with <<<<<<< lines, and exits with the number of conflicts.
git merge-file deploy/runners.yaml \ "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" \ "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" Repeat for the other files you copied. Take the entrypoint and the distributor script of the new release unless you edited them, and rename their Swarm configs as Upgrade to a new release says.
Check deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints and deploy.resources, the runner version pin with its SHA-256 values (a release changes them together), and the token proxy image (a release names it by digest).
Check the result.
docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null Deploy with the same list of -c files as before.
docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Swarm replaces the token proxy and updates the runner services one replica at a time. While the proxy is replaced, no new job is claimed, and every runner that had already claimed stays refused (Restart the proxy). To roll back, deploy the previous copy.
data.verify-a-release#Verify a release:
CircleCI signs SHA256SUMS with the OIDC token of the CircleCI job that makes the release. No signing key is stored anywhere. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksums prove that your download is the file the job made. You need cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested), curl, jq, and GNU coreutils, in a bash shell. On Windows, see Verify a release.
Set version to the number of the latest release without the v, and read the release notes.
version=$(curl -fsSLI -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest) version=${version##*/v} The next block runs in a subshell and stops at the first failing check. It checks:
The signature: this project’s CircleCI pipeline signed SHA256SUMS. The ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main. The long string in the block is the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by refs/heads/main. The checksum: the bundle is in the signed list. Only a bundle that passes all three is unpacked.
