( set -euo pipefail base="https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v${version}" curl -fsSLO "${base}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" \ -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS" \ -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json" cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com" hex=$(jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ | base64 -d | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n') grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' <<< "${hex}" \ && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop"; exit 1; } sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing tar -xzf "machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" echo "RELEASE VERIFIED" ) Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, including no output, means the release is not verified: delete the files and start again, or ask in an issue. Then change into the bundle:
cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}" The token proxy image has its own signature: Verify the token proxy image has the commands.
The checks establish less than a review does:
A valid signature and refs/heads/main mean that a job of this CircleCI project ran for main and made these files. Whether anyone can change main without a review is a setting of the organization that owns the repository (A ruleset for main says what the project asks for).
The identity is the CircleCI project (7bbdbb66-...) and the pipeline definition (8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60) of the pipeline of machine runner swarm, with the issuer https://oidc.circleci.com. Sigstore records every signature in a public transparency log. If the project or its pipeline definition is re-created, the definition ID changes, and this page gives the new value.
To see the ref of a certificate, print it. The last line ends with the ref, and a release comes from refs/heads/main.
jq -r '.verificationMaterial.certificate.rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \ | openssl x509 -inform DER -noout -text | grep -A1 '1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14:'
data.verify-the-deployment#Verify the deploym:
List the services. Each shows the running and desired replicas.
docker stack services runners ID NAME MODE REPLICAS IMAGE ... runners_linux-default replicated 2/2 cimg/base:2026.10 ... runners_runner-distributor global 1/1 alpine:3 ... runners_token-proxy replicated 1/1 ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:... The distributor has one task for each Linux node (a microVM node has none): 1/1 on one node, 3/3 on three.
Check the tasks. A task in the Running state is a runner that polls CircleCI.
docker service ps runners_linux-default Check that the distributor installed the runner. Its log has a line such as runner-distributor: [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13: circleci-runner 3.1.13 linux/amd64 for each node (See what runs).
docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor Check that the runners connected. Each replica is listed as online, named -- (for example node1-linux-default-1). The web app shows the same under Runners.
circleci runner instance list --org --resource-class /linux-default Run a job with examples/linux-hello.yml (the quickstart shows it), twice. After each job, Swarm shows a new task for the slot. The job clean-check in examples/linux-jobs.yml fails if anything from an earlier job is still present.

data:
This page deploys CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server. Every job runs in a new Windows Server Core container, and Swarm replaces the container after the job. The steps cover one host (Multi-node clusters adds more). For a first run, Quickstart on Windows Server is shorter.
Note Tested against CircleCI cloud only (What is tested). Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add nodes or scale to the queue. On Kubernetes, use container runner.
The steps: start or join a swarm, label the node, create the secrets, deploy. The optional setup helper runs most of them.
Important The services run the stock Server Core image, and no image is built. On Windows, change a class only while it is idle (why).
data.1-create-the-resource-classes#1. Create:
Create a namespace if your organization has none.
circleci namespace create <NAMESPACE> --org <ORG> Create one resource class for each service in the stack files. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped windows\stack\runners.yaml has the service windows-default and deploys on its own.
circleci runner resource-class create <NAMESPACE>/windows-default --org <ORG> --generate-token The command prints the token once: store it in your secret manager. The optional add-on files in the same directory add windows-custom (custom-image.yaml), windows-persistent (persistent.yaml), windows-docker-build (docker-build.yaml) and windows-default-ssh (ssh-rerun.yaml, untested). Create the classes you plan to use.
data.2-prepare-each-host#2. Prepare each host:
Run these steps in an elevated PowerShell on every host, before you start Swarm: the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init, and the pull needs it.
Confirm that Docker runs Windows containers. The command prints windows.
docker info --format '{{.OSType}}' Pull the base image of the shipped services once, so the first task does not wait for it. A Server 2025 host runs ltsc2022 images too, so this is the image for both hosts. Pull ltsc2025 as well only for a service that you put on that image.
docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 On the host that runs the token proxy (a manager, by default), pull the image that your stack file names, or build your own (The token proxy image). A release bundle names a tag and a digest, and latest is a different image.
docker pull ((Select-String -Path windows\stack\runners.yaml -Pattern 'MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE:-([^}]+)\}').Matches[0].Groups[1].Value)
data.3-start-swarm-and-label-the-node#3. Star:
On the first host, start Swarm. Always pass --advertise-addr with the IPv4 address of the host: a plain docker swarm init fails on some hosts with could not find the system's IP address. For more than one node, see Multi-node clusters.
docker swarm init --advertise-addr <HOST_IPV4_ADDRESS> Label the node with the image tags it can run. On Server 2022 and 2025:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true <NODE_NAME> On Server 2025 only, add the second label:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true <NODE_NAME> On a single node, the token proxy needs no label: it runs on the manager, and the jobs run there too. In a cluster, give the proxy a node of its own: label it machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true, and runner services never run there, so a job never shares a node with the proxy. Do not set the label on the only node of a swarm, because no runner would be placed. If the managers are Linux hosts, or there are several managers, also pin the proxy to a Windows node with the placement in the environment of docker stack deploy:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <NODE_NAME> $env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT = 'node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' Without a matching node the proxy stays pending and no runner can claim (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). The optional classes need one more label each, on the nodes that run them:
Class Label windows-docker-build machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true windows-persistent machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true
data.4-create-the-secrets#4. Create the secre:
Create one secret for each service you deploy, named -token, including each optional class (windows-persistent-token too: persistent.yaml declares it as external, so the deploy fails without it). It is a runner config file that holds only the token:
api: auth_token: The token proxy mounts the secrets of the proxied classes, and those runners never see them. The persistent class is the exception (The persistent class). The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a dummy token in the same format (the setup helper creates it). Swarm mounts it at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml, and the runner reads it with --config. Every other runner setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable in the stack file.
This block asks for the token with hidden input and passes the config to docker secret create on stdin, so no file with the token is written on the host. Repeat the first part for each class, with its name in $class. Create the placeholder once.
$class = 'windows-default' $secure = Read-Host -Prompt "Runner token for $class" -AsSecureString $bstr = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($secure) try { $token = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($bstr) } finally { [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($bstr) } if (-not $token) { throw "no token entered for $class" } "api:`n auth_token: $token`n" | docker secret create "$class-token" - Remove-Variable token "api:`n auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder`n" | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token - Windows does not support the uid, gid and mode options of secrets: only administrators and SYSTEM can read the file inside the container, and jobs run as an administrator. Swarm also writes the secret in clear text to the disk of the container until it stops, which is a Swarm limitation on Windows (Linux keeps it in memory). Enable BitLocker on the Docker volume (Token model on each OS).
data.5-review-the-stack-files#5. Review the s:
Copy windows\stack to a directory of your own, deploy\, and keep it under version control. From here on you check and deploy your copies and never the files under windows\stack. For a first run, change nothing.
Copy-Item -Recurse windows\stack deploy Check that the file parses. This needs no running Swarm.
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null The directory holds the stack files and runner-distributor.ps1, the script that runners.yaml ships as a Swarm config (file: runner-distributor.ps1): keep it next to runners.yaml. Review these first (Resource classes has the details):
Service File Purpose runner-distributor-windows runners.yaml Installs and upgrades the runner and Git on every Windows node. Keep it in your copy windows-default runners.yaml Stock Server Core image, two replicas windows-custom custom-image.yaml Your own image on top of stock Server Core (Images). It has a placeholder image that you replace windows-persistent persistent.yaml A long-lived runner with a named volume (Persistent mode) windows-docker-build docker-build.yaml Builds Windows images with the host engine (Docker builds) windows-default-ssh ssh-rerun.yaml Rerun job with SSH, port 54782. Untested on Windows (Rerun job with SSH) runners.yaml needs the secrets windows-default-token and runner-placeholder-token. Each add-on file needs its own -token. The distributor settings (the runner version, a mirror, an explicit SHA-256 list) are variables of docker stack deploy and need no edit (Upgrade the runner on Windows). For a class on the ltsc2025 image, copy a service under a new name and resource class, use the ltsc2025 image tag, and set the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true. Add each optional file with another -c flag, and pass the same list on every deploy (how the files merge). Each add-on file repeats the anchors of runners.yaml and declares the volume runner-bin, so it also loads alone: change a common setting in every file you use. To check the optional files, pass them all in the order you deploy them:
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml -c deploy\persistent.yaml -c deploy\docker-build.yaml | Out-Null For the keys that Windows honors and ignores, see Stack keys on Windows.
data.6-deploy-the-stack#6. Deploy the stack:
Deploy your copy from step 5:
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners To add optional classes, pass your copies after runners.yaml with more -c flags, for example your own image on top of stock Server Core:
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml runners The runner-distributor-windows service starts on every Windows node. It downloads the pinned runner and the pinned portable Git (about 60 MB, 406 MB unpacked), verifies their SHA-256 checksums (the runner against the values the stack file carries, not CircleCI’s manifest), installs them into the per-node volume runner-bin, and flips two links. The runner services mount the volume read-only twice: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe. The stock Server Core image needs no changes.
On a new node the first runner tasks fail with cannot access path ... \current until the distributor has flipped the link, which takes a few minutes for the first download. Swarm starts the next task after the restart delay of 10 seconds, so nothing needs to be done. Watch the distributor:
docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows
data.get-the-files#Get the files:
Use a release (recommended) or clone the repository at a release tag. Paths on this page are relative to the root of either. The GitHub release has the bundle machine-runner-swarm-.zip, and the Linux page lists every file of a release. To verify the signature first, see Verify a release.
git clone --branch <RELEASE_TAG> https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm.git cd machine-runner-swarm
data.image-tags-and-host-builds#Image tags an:
With process isolation, the image build must be the host build or an older one. Label every node with the image tags it can run: a service is placed on a node that carries the label of its image tag.
Host Images it can run Node labels Windows Server 2022 ltsc2022 only machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true Windows Server 2025 ltsc2025 and ltsc2022 machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true and machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true The shipped services use ltsc2022 images, so they run on 2022 and 2025 nodes. A service on an ltsc2025 image requires machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true, so it runs on 2025 nodes only. A mismatch that the labels do not catch fails with 0xc0370101.
data.install-cosign#Install cosign:
cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x verifies the release (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). Download the executable and the checksum list of the cosign release, compare the checksum, and put the file in a directory on your PATH:
$cosign = '3.1.3' $u = "https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v$cosign" Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign-windows-amd64.exe" -OutFile cosign.exe Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign_checksums.txt" -OutFile cosign_checksums.txt $want = ((Get-Content cosign_checksums.txt | Where-Object { $_ -match '\scosign-windows-amd64\.exe$' }) -split '\s+')[0] if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath cosign.exe).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw 'the checksum of cosign.exe does not match: stop' } .\cosign.exe version This checks the file against a list from the same place: it catches a damaged download, not a compromised release page. Your own package manager is another source.
data.next#Next: Uninstall. On Windows, stop only an idle class (why) Troubleshooting: the most common problems are an image tag that does not match the host build, a distributor that has not installed the runner yet, and a job that ends about 5 seconds after a stop. A task also stays pending when no node carries the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 label (or windows-ltsc2025, for a service on an ltsc2025 image) Concepts Resource classes Security Operations Machine runner 3 on Windows
data.optional-use-the-setup-helper#Optional::
windows\Setup.ps1 checks the host, starts Swarm on request, labels the node, creates the secrets, and deploys. It does not install the runner: the distributor service of the stack does that on every node. It runs in an elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session and is safe to run again. It prints CHECK PASS or FAIL for each preflight check (administrator, Windows Server build, Windows-container mode, Docker 28.0 or later, Swarm manager), and ends with Next: and the steps still to do, or Check: and the commands that watch the start.
Parameter Effect -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr Creates a Swarm when none exists, and waits until the node is a manager. The address is needed only then: on an active Swarm, -InitSwarm changes nothing -Class , Asks for each token with hidden input and creates the secret -token. An existing secret stays unchanged (placeholder) With -Class or -Deploy, it also creates the secret runner-placeholder-token with a dummy token, which every runner reads -Deploy Runs docker stack deploy with -StackFile (one or more files, runners.yaml first) and -StackName (default runners). Without -StackFile it deploys the shipped windows\stack\runners.yaml as it is, which suits a first run. Once you keep copies as in step 5, pass them. It prints the files it deploys The helper labels the node from the host build: windows-ltsc2022=true on Server 2022, and both windows-ltsc2022=true and windows-ltsc2025=true on Server 2025 (machine-runner-swarm. prefix). It supports Server 2022 and 2025 only, and does not add the labels of the optional classes. The distributor reads its settings from the environment of -Deploy.
The first command is a first run with the shipped runners.yaml. The second deploys your copy from step 5, with its optional file.
.\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr 10.0.0.5 -Class windows-default -Deploy .\windows\Setup.ps1 -Class windows-default,windows-custom -StackFile .\deploy\runners.yaml,.\deploy\custom-image.yaml -Deploy
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known.
The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. It can run on your workstation. Pass --org (a slug such as gh/my-org, or a UUID): without it the CLI uses the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours.
One or more Windows Server hosts (table below). The host cannot be a domain controller.
Docker Engine 28.0 or later (CLI and engine), in Windows-container mode, with the Windows Containers feature (enabling it restarts the host). The stack files mount a subpath of a volume (current and git\current), which older CLIs and engines ignore: the runner would not start. CI runs Docker 29.4.0 on Windows, and windows\Setup.ps1 checks the version. To install both, download and run the Install-DockerCE sample of the Microsoft Windows Containers repository, pinned here to a commit. Read it first. It installs the latest Docker CE, and enabling the feature restarts the host.
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/Windows-Containers/9fd4c4d85597ce75834f4e1cd21695c34642de3d/helpful_tools/Install-DockerCE/install-docker-ce.ps1' -OutFile install-docker-ce.ps1 .\install-docker-ce.ps1 An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session.
A host clock synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts.
Outbound HTTPS from each host to the hosts in Egress hosts: circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com (the runner and its manifest), github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com (Git and 7-Zip), mcr.microsoft.com (the base image), and Docker Hub (the token proxy image). What needs internet lists everything. Hosts without internet access are not tested (mirrors).
Disk: servercore is about 2.2 GB compressed. Each container shows 20 GB free on C: by default. To raise the limit, add "storage-opts": ["size=60GB"] to C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json. Every finished container keeps its layer until Swarm prunes it.
CPU and memory: each windows-default replica reserves 2 CPUs and 4 GB, so two replicas reserve 4 CPUs and 8 GB. The proxy and the distributor reserve nothing but can use 1 CPU each. Runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan must cover your replicas (Size the limits).
Windows Server Machine runner 3 Status 2025 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2025 2022 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2022 2019 Compatible Untested here: the stack files have no label or placement for it 2016 and older Not compatible Not supported
data.self-hosted-runner-terms-agreement#Self-: An organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms before you install self-hosted runners through the web app. Through the CLI, you agree by installing and using them (details). Whether the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered is for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy holds your class tokens (The token proxy). On Windows it is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy of Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs), which the stack file token-proxy-windows pulls on deploy: a static binary on Nano Server, for windows/amd64. The name is not the trust root: the signature check is. One tag also holds the Linux images, and a manifest list holds one Windows image for Server 2022 and one for Server 2025, so Docker picks the one of the host. Tags, pinning and the signature are the same as on Linux: The token proxy image and Verify the token proxy image.
The image runs as ContainerAdministrator, as the stock Server Core image does, because ContainerUser of Nano Server cannot write to the volume that keeps the state of the proxy.
There is no windows/arm64 image, because CI has no Windows on Arm host to build and test one on. In a cluster with Windows on Arm nodes, pin the proxy to a windows/amd64 node with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT (Multi-node clusters). A cluster of only Windows on Arm nodes needs an image of your own: build the proxy with GOARCH=arm64, build proxy\Dockerfile.windows on an arm64 host with an arm64 Nano Server image as --build-arg BASE=, and name it with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE.
To use another image (development, an air gap), set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE in the environment of docker stack deploy. The image must be on the node that runs the proxy: a local build exists only where you built it. This builds one from a checkout: build the binary on any host with Go, then build the image on the Windows host whose build matches the base image.
$env:GOOS = 'windows'; $env:GOARCH = 'amd64'; $env:CGO_ENABLED = '0' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path build | Out-Null Push-Location proxy; go build -trimpath -o ..\build\machine-runner-swarm-proxy.exe .\cmd\machine-runner-swarm-proxy; Pop-Location docker build -f proxy\Dockerfile.windows -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev build $env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE = 'machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev'
data.upgrade#Upgrade:
The distributor pins the exact runner version that this release tests, with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, and the nodes keep it until you change it. 3.1, 3 or current (weaker: they trust the hash of the manifest) follow CircleCI’s manifest and check every 24 hours. A pin of your own is two variables of docker stack deploy: the version and its SHA-256 values (or manifest for an exact version without a list). Running jobs keep their version, and the runner services never restart (Upgrade the runner on Windows).
A new release changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy\ is not updated by itself. To merge, with git from Git for Windows or another diff and merge tool:
Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.
Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old directory is the base of the merge.
Set the two versions, and see what changed between the releases.
$old = '' $new = '' Merge each file that differs into your copy. git merge-file edits the file in place, marks conflicts with <<<<<<< lines, and exits with the number of conflicts.
git diff --no-index "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack" git merge-file deploy\runners.yaml "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack\runners.yaml" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack\runners.yaml" Repeat for the other files you copied. Take runner-distributor.ps1 of the new release unless you edited it (Upgrade to a new release explains the names of the Swarm configs).
Check deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints and deploy.resources, the runner version pin with its SHA-256 values (a release changes them together), and the token proxy image (a release names it by digest).
Check the result.
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null Deploy while the classes are idle (Stop a busy Windows container), with the same list of -c files as before.
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners To roll back, deploy the previous copy.
data.verify-a-release#Verify a release:
CircleCI signs the file SHA256SUMS of each release with the OIDC token of the job that makes the release. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksum proves that your download is the file that the job made. The Linux page explains what the signature proves, and what it does not.
Set $version to the number of the latest release without the v, and read the release notes.
$uri = (Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri 'https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/latest').BaseResponse.ResponseUri.AbsoluteUri $version = $uri -replace '^.*/v', '' $base = "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/machine-runner-swarm/releases/download/v$version" $zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip" The next block stops at the first failing check. The variables are set outside it, because & runs the block in a scope of its own. It checks:
The signature: this project’s CircleCI pipeline signed SHA256SUMS. The ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main. The long string in the block is the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by refs/heads/main. The checksum: the bundle is in the signed list. Only a bundle that passes all three is unpacked.
& { $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' foreach ($f in $zip, 'SHA256SUMS', 'SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json') { Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$base/$f" -OutFile $f } cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json ` --certificate-identity 'https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60' ` --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://oidc.circleci.com' if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'the signature does not verify: stop' } $material = (Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | ConvertFrom-Json).verificationMaterial if ($material.certificate) { $cert = $material.certificate.rawBytes } else { $cert = $material.x509CertificateChain.certificates[0].rawBytes } $hex = -join ([Convert]::FromBase64String($cert) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') }) if ($hex -notmatch '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e') { throw 'NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop' } $want = ((Get-Content SHA256SUMS | Where-Object { $_ -match "\s$([regex]::Escape($zip))$" }) -split '\s+')[0] if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $zip).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw "the checksum of $zip is not the signed one: stop" } Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath . 'RELEASE VERIFIED' } Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, including no output, means the release is not verified: delete the files and start again, or ask in an issue. Then change into the bundle:
cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version" The token proxy image has its own signature: Verify the token proxy image has the commands.
data.verify-the-deployment#Verify the deploym:
List the services and tasks. The service runners_runner-distributor-windows shows one replica for each Windows node.
docker stack services runners docker stack ps runners --no-trunc Check that the runners connected. Each replica is listed as online, named --. The web app shows the same under Runners.
circleci runner instance list --org <ORG> --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/windows-default Run a job. The quickstart has a complete config, and examples/windows-job.yml has more steps. Run the workflow twice: the two runs print different values for $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID, because each job runs in a new container.
data.what-jobs-can-use#What jobs can use: The default shell is Git Bash (bash -eo pipefail). Set shell: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass for Windows PowerShell 5.1, or shell: cmd.exe, per job or step. The working directory is C:\cci\w, and the task agent lives in C:\cci\agent. The PATH of the service reaches every step. checkout, caches, test results and artifacts need Git and outbound access. Workspaces use the tar and gzip from the mounted Git. OpenID Connect tokens need a writable %TEMP%. The stack enables Git long paths through the environment. The registry value LongPathsEnabled is not set: a job that needs long paths for other tools sets it itself, or in its own image. Not supported: desktop or UI automation, Docker commands in jobs (except the opt-in docker-build class), and service containers. Not tested: add_ssh_keys, Hyper-V isolation, group managed service accounts, and proxies. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER of the Linux entrypoint do not exist on Windows, and Windows ignores them. There is no step-down.

data:
This page runs the stack on a cluster of Linux amd64, Linux arm64 and Windows nodes. One Swarm schedules every replica, and labels decide which node may run which resource class.
A one-node install that follows the quickstart cannot grow: its swarm listens on the loopback address. Start a cluster here, with a routable address, and use the install pages (Linux, Windows Server) for the per-node steps.
Layout Hosts Use it for One node 1 A trial. Jobs and the token proxy share the host Small 2: a manager with the proxy label, one worker Jobs on the worker. No manager failover Production 4 or more: three managers (one with the proxy label, the others drained), and workers Quorum survives the loss of one manager. The proxy runs on one node: if it is lost, label another (The node of the proxy) flowchart LR subgraph nodes["Nodes and their labels"] A["linux-alinux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"] B["linux-blinux, aarch64machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"] C["linux-clinux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy"] D["linux-d (worker)linux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true"] W["win-awindowsmachine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true"] end subgraph services["Services and their constraints"] S1["linux-buildos == linuxzone == build"] S2["linux-arm64arch == aarch64"] S3["linux-deployzone == deploy"] S4["linux-docker-buildrole == workerdocker-build == true"] S5["windows-defaultos == windowsmachine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 == true"] end S1 -.-> A S1 -.-> B S2 -.-> B S3 -.-> C S4 -.-> D S5 -.-> WA dotted line means that the node satisfies every constraint of the service, so Swarm may place a replica there. A service stays pending when no node matches.
data.arm-nodes#Arm nodes:
The runner-distributor service reads the architecture of the node and installs the arm64 runner build on an Arm node. Swarm reports Arm nodes as aarch64 and Intel and AMD nodes as x86_64.
Give each architecture its own resource class, for example linux-arm64, constrained with node.platform.arch == aarch64: a job cannot pick an architecture inside a class that spans both. Use an image that publishes an arm64 variant (check with docker buildx imagetools inspect ).
data.built-in-node-properties#Built-in node p: Property Values node.platform.os linux, windows node.platform.arch x86_64, aarch64 node.hostname The hostname of the node node.role manager, worker
data.create-the-swarm#Create the swarm:
Initialize Swarm on the first manager with an address that the other nodes can reach (not the loopback address of the single-node install).
docker swarm init --advertise-addr --task-history-limit 2 --default-addr-pool --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24 Two options matter for this stack, and neither is the default:
--task-history-limit 2. Every finished job ends a task, and Swarm keeps the last 5 tasks of each slot, with their containers and disk, unless you lower it (Free disk space). Change it later with docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2. --default-addr-pool. Each Linux class gets its own /24 overlay network from the default pool of Swarm, 10.0.0.0/8. Choose a pool that does not overlap your own networks, because an overlap makes tasks unreachable in ways that are hard to see. Choose a range that none of your networks uses, for example a free /16 from 10.0.0.0/8: it gives 256 networks. You can set the pool only when you create the swarm. If you started with the loopback address, run docker stack rm runners and docker swarm leave --force, initialize again, and recreate the secrets.
Get the join command for each node type on a manager. Run the printed command (docker swarm join --token :2377) on the node.
docker swarm join-token worker docker swarm join-token manager A join token grants cluster membership: keep it secret, and rotate it with docker swarm join-token --rotate worker when it leaks. Confirm the nodes from a manager.
docker node ls
data.encrypted-class-networks#Encrypted class:
The Linux stack files create the class networks as encrypted overlays: driver: overlay with driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}. The runners reach the token proxy over http://token-proxy:8080, and that traffic carries task tokens, the job configuration with the secrets of its contexts, and step output. In clear text, anyone on the network could read it or inject packets into the overlay, which the source-address guarantee of the proxy depends on. Swarm encrypts the VXLAN traffic between nodes with IPsec instead. A node that cannot reach another over ESP drops that traffic, which looks like a runner that cannot find token-proxy: if a runner cannot reach the proxy from another node, check ESP first.
Cost. IPsec costs CPU on every node and some throughput. A single-node Swarm needs nothing open. Opt out. If the network between your nodes is yours (a private network, or a link that you encrypt another way), delete driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"} from every class network of your copy of the Linux stack files (runners.yaml and the add-on files you use). A Swarm network cannot change after it exists: run docker stack rm runners, wait until the networks are gone (docker network ls), and deploy again. Without the option, ESP is not needed. Windows. Docker does not support encrypted overlay networks for Windows containers, so the Windows stack files set no driver_opts, and their overlay carries the traffic of the Windows classes and token-proxy-windows in clear text between nodes. Keep the Windows nodes on a network that you trust, or encrypt the link at the host (for example with Windows Firewall connection security rules for IPsec). All Windows classes share the default overlay of the stack.
data.inter-node-ports#Inter-node ports:
Swarm needs these ports between all nodes of the cluster. Open them only for the addresses of cluster nodes.
Port Protocol Purpose Nodes 2377 TCP Cluster management Managers only receive it 7946 TCP and UDP Node discovery All nodes 4789 UDP Overlay network (VXLAN) All nodes IP protocol 50 (ESP) IPsec Encrypted overlay networks (the Linux class networks). It is a protocol, not a port All nodes with Linux services The runner containers need no inbound ports, and the stack publishes none. Outbound HTTPS from each node is the only other requirement (Egress hosts).
Ubuntu with ufw:
sudo ufw allow from to any port 2377 proto tcp sudo ufw allow from to any port 7946 sudo ufw allow from to any port 4789 proto udp sudo ufw allow from proto esp RHEL with firewalld:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --new-zone=swarm sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-source= sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-port=2377/tcp --add-port=7946/tcp --add-port=7946/udp --add-port=4789/udp sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-protocol=esp sudo firewall-cmd --reload In a cloud, add a security group rule for protocol number 50 (ESP) with the security group of the nodes as the source. Most consoles list it as “Custom protocol 50” or “ESP”.
Windows Server:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm TCP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 2377,7946 -RemoteAddress <CLUSTER_SUBNET> New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm UDP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 7946,4789 -RemoteAddress <CLUSTER_SUBNET> On a Windows host with a single network adapter, an existing transparent network can block the creation of the overlay networks: see the Microsoft documentation on Windows container networking if overlay creation fails.
data.keep-the-docker-build-node-to-itself#Kee: A job on a docker-build class controls the whole Docker engine of its node, so it can enter every other container there and read the tokens of any class that runs on that node. The stack files keep the other classes off that node: every runner service except the docker-build ones carries the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build != true (a node without the label matches it, because Swarm treats a missing label as “not equal”). runner-distributor has no such constraint, because the docker-build class needs the runner on its node too. A node that gets the label stops running those services: Swarm starts replacements on other nodes, or leaves them pending. Add the same constraint to every service you write yourself.
data.labels-and-constraints#Labels and constr:
A service constraint says where Swarm may place a replica, and all constraints of a service must hold. Add them under deploy.placement.constraints. The spread: node.id preference, which the shipped stack files set, spreads the replicas evenly over the matching nodes.
deploy: placement: constraints: - node.platform.os == linux - node.platform.arch == aarch64 - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == build preferences: - spread: node.id
data.labels-used-by-the-stack#Labels used by:
Set a label with docker node update --label-add = , and remove it with --label-rm . Constraints on labels have the form node.labels. == .
Label Value Used by machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 true Every shipped Windows service, which uses ltsc2022 images. Set on Server 2022 and 2025 nodes machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 true Services on an ltsc2025 image. Set on Server 2025 nodes only machine-runner-swarm.zone A network zone name Services that must run in one zone. A commented example sits in the Linux placement block machine-runner-swarm.docker-build true The docker-build services (pattern A) (Docker builds) machine-runner-swarm.container-mode true The container agent of container mode (experimental), on workers only. The token proxy stays off container-mode nodes machine-runner-swarm.proxy true The node that runs the token proxy, in a cluster. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' the proxy runs only there, and no runner service runs on a node with this label. On a single node, set no label (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves) machine-runner-swarm.microvm true The microVM services, on nodes whose Docker daemon runs every container in a Kata microVM. Every other service stays off these nodes (MicroVM jobs) machine-runner-swarm.class. true Pins a service to the labeled nodes. windows-persistent uses machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent. linux-persistent pins itself with node.hostname instead
data.linux-nodes#Linux nodes:
On each node:
Install Docker Engine and confirm that the clock is synchronized (Prepare each node). Open the ports in Inter-node ports. Run the join command. Nothing else is installed on the node. The runner-distributor service is global, so Swarm starts it on the new node by itself, and it installs the runner into the volume runner-bin (it skips a node labeled machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true: the microVM classes download their own runner). A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for it.
data.managers-and-quorum#Managers and quorum:
Managers keep the cluster state, including every Swarm secret, in an encrypted Raft log. Each manager holds a copy.
Use one manager for a small installation without availability needs, three to survive the loss of one, or five to survive the loss of two. Use an odd number: quorum is a majority. Keep the managers on reliable, low-latency links. Quorum matters more here than in a typical Swarm. Every job ends with a runner exit, and only a manager with quorum can create the replacement task. Without quorum, running jobs finish but the runners are not replaced, so the capacity drops to zero.
Keep jobs off managers when you can: a container breakout on a manager exposes the tokens of every class. In a cluster, label the node that runs the token proxy (a manager) and tell the deploy about it. Runner services never run on a node with that label, so no job shares a node with the class tokens.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Keep the variable with your other deploy variables (Keep the deploy variables in version control): a deploy without it puts the proxy back on any manager. Drain the other managers so that they run no tasks.
docker node update --availability drain Warning The token proxy needs a node that is not drained. token-proxy runs on a manager by default (node.role == manager), or on the labeled node. If you drain every manager, or the labeled node, the proxy stays Pending (no suitable node) and no runner can claim a job, with no other error: the runners only log 502 or a refused connection to token-proxy. The same happens when the managers are Linux hosts and the proxy is the Windows one (token-proxy-windows also defaults to a manager, and a Windows task cannot run on a Linux manager), and when a Windows-only swarm has no Windows manager. Label a Windows node for it (a worker works), and in a mixed cluster label one Linux and one Windows node, because each proxy keeps to its own operating system. Never drain the labeled node without the steps in The node of the proxy. A proxy on a worker still holds every class token, so choose a node that runs no jobs.
On a single-node Swarm the only node is a manager and runs the replicas and the proxy: set no label. Never use the Docker socket classes (pattern A) there (Docker builds).
data.mixed-architectures#Mixed architectures:
One cluster can have x86_64 and aarch64 nodes. Nothing else is needed on the nodes.
Which build a node gets. Each runner-distributor task downloads circleci-runner_linux_.tar.gz for its own node and checks its SHA-256 against the entry of that architecture in the manifest. If you set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, list the hash of every architecture in the cluster. A tarball that does not match installs nothing on that node, and the other nodes still install. Placement. A class without an architecture constraint can run on both kinds of node. Add node.platform.arch == aarch64 or x86_64 to the constraints of the classes that need one. When the nodes of that architecture are drained or gone, the class stays Pending with no suitable node: it never moves to the other architecture. What is tested. linux/tests/mixed-arch.sh (the optional CI job linux-mixed-arch, see CI) deploys the shipped stack file on an amd64 manager and an arm64 worker. It checks that each node installs the runner of its own architecture, that a tarball that does not match its manifest entry installs nothing on that node only, and that classes constrained by node.platform.arch run only on their architecture, also when the other node is drained. Emulated, not real. That arm64 worker is a docker:dind container under QEMU emulation on an x86_64 host. The test proves the install, the verification and the placement logic, not the speed or system call behavior of an Arm node. IPsec on overlays does not work under emulation, so it deploys the plain-overlay copy of the stack files (the opt-out of Encrypted class networks), and placement.sh tests the encrypted files on two nodes. Real arm64 nodes are tested by the single-node jobs linux-arm64 and e2e-linux-arm64 (a real runner on an Arm VM).
data.network-zones#Network zones:
Use the label machine-runner-swarm.zone when your nodes sit in different network zones, for example a build network and a deploy network with different firewall rules or egress addresses.
Label each node with its zone.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=build linux-a docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy linux-c Copy a service for each zone, give each copy its own resource class, secret and name, and add the constraint.
linux-deploy: # ... deploy: placement: constraints: - node.platform.os == linux - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == deploy A job picks the zone by picking the resource class. Do not use zones to balance capacity: use replicas and spread.
data.next#Next: Resource classes Operations, including how to drain a node for patching Security
data.plan-the-cluster#Plan the cluster: Node type Role Needs Manager Holds the cluster state and every secret. Schedules tasks Docker Engine. Linux managers can manage Windows workers Linux worker Runs Linux services Docker Engine. The runner-distributor service installs the runner for the architecture of the node Windows worker Runs Windows services Docker Engine in Windows-container mode, the ltsc2022 base image, the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc* labels. Nothing else: the distributor installs the runner and Git
data.registry-needs#Registry needs:
Swarm does not share images between nodes: each node pulls the image of a task from a registry the first time the task lands there.
Every node must reach the registry of every image that a service on that node uses (Egress hosts). Your own image must be in a registry that all nodes of its OS can reach (Images). For a private registry, run docker login on the manager and deploy with docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth. Pin images by digest, for example cimg/base:2026.10@sha256:, so every node runs the same content. Tags such as 21.0 move. Pull large images ahead of time (a Windows servercore image is about 2.2 GB compressed). Public registries apply pull rate limits: a mirror or an authenticated pull avoids failed pulls. runner-distributor runs the stock alpine:3 image on every Linux node. If the nodes cannot reach Docker Hub, mirror it and change image in your copy of the stack file. Copy it with its digest (docker buildx imagetools create keeps it), so the pin holds. The token proxy runs from ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy. Mirror it with its signature (cosign copy), pin the digest in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE, and keep that in your deploy file (Upgrade the token proxy). A manager that cannot reach the registry cannot resolve a tag to a digest on deploy. Use docker stack deploy --resolve-image never, or images that you pinned by digest and mirrored. A site with no route to the internet also needs the runner download and the task agent (CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet).
data.verify-the-placement#Verify the placemen: docker node ls docker node inspect --format '{{ .Spec.Labels }}' docker service ps runners_linux-default The NODE column of docker service ps shows where each replica runs. A task that stays Pending shows the reason in the ERROR column, for example no suitable node (scheduling constraints not satisfied on 2 nodes) (A task stays pending).
data.windows-nodes#Windows nodes:
On each node:
Install Docker Engine in Windows-container mode and the Windows Containers feature.
Pull the images before the join (Prepare each host). The runner and Git are not staged: the service runner-distributor-windows installs them after the join.
Open the ports in Inter-node ports.
Run the join command.
From a manager, label the node with the image tags it can run. A Server 2025 node also gets windows-ltsc2025, because it runs ltsc2022 images too.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true The labels are required, because the image build must be the host build or an older one (Image tags and host builds).
Deploy the Linux and Windows files into the same stack name. The service names differ, so they do not collide. Do not use docker stack deploy --prune there: it removes the services of the other file.
Mixed Linux and Windows clusters are tested by hand, not in CI. The constraints on node.platform.os keep each service on its own operating system. A cluster of a Linux manager and a Windows Server 2022 worker ran real CircleCI jobs on both operating systems, with both runner distributors and an overlay network between them. CI tests each operating system on its own Swarm, because the Linux and Windows VMs of CI cannot reach each other. A mixed cluster needs the ports 2377, 7946 and 4789 open between its nodes (Inter-node ports), and a Linux manager that both stack files are deployed from.

data: Operations: Runbooks for status and logs, capacity, upgrades, token rotation, proxy restarts, and node drains, then reference for monitoring, backups, compatibility, and uninstall. Troubleshooting: Symptoms, causes and fixes for the Docker Swarm runner stack on Linux and Windows, with the error text to search for.

Day-2 tasks for a running stack: the common runbooks first, then reference. Commands use the stack name runners and the shipped service names, and run on a manager node.
Task Section See what runs, read logs Check status and logs Add replicas Capacity and concurrency Change the runner, proxy or images Upgrade the runner and images Replace a class token Rotate a runner token Restart the token proxy Restart the proxy Patch or reboot a node Drain a node for patching On Windows, change a class only while it is idle (why).
data.a-claim-whose-outcome-is-unknown#A claim: A claim can reach CircleCI while its answer is lost: the connection resets, or CircleCI sends no response headers within 60 seconds. The proxy cannot tell whether a task was handed over, so it latches the runner (fail closed): the runner gets an error and no task, and every later claim of that container is refused (403) until Swarm replaces it. The cost is one idle runner. If CircleCI had allocated a task to it, the task never runs: rerun the job if it does not end. A claim that never reached CircleCI (the proxy cannot connect) is not latched.
data.a-windows-node#A Windows node:
Use pause, which keeps new tasks away and stops nothing:
docker node update --availability pause <NODE> docker node ps <NODE> --filter desired-state=running A running job keeps its container. Each replica that finishes exits, and Swarm starts its replacement elsewhere, so the node empties by itself. An idle replica exits only at its idle timeout (1 hour) and can claim a job until then, so the upper bound is the idle timeout plus the longest job. When the second command prints nothing, drain the node (no job is left to kill), patch it and set it active.
data.back-up-the-managers-and-recover#Back up:
The cluster state is /var/lib/docker/swarm on each manager. It holds the Raft log with every Swarm secret, so the backup holds every runner token. Keep it like a password vault and delete old copies.
Docker stops on the manager you copy, so the others must keep the quorum: the method needs a second manager. With one manager, keep your stack files and deploy variables in version control and rely on the redeploy below.
If the managers use autolock, save the key: docker swarm unlock-key.
Choose a manager that is not the leader (docker node ls, MANAGER STATUS) and does not run token-proxy. Use three managers so the quorum stands while one is stopped.
If it runs jobs, drain it first and wait until its tasks are gone, because stopping Docker ends every container on the node (Drain a node for patching).
Stop Docker, copy, start Docker, and set the node active:
sudo systemctl stop docker sudo tar -czf swarm-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /var/lib/docker swarm sudo systemctl start docker docker node update --availability active For this stack, disaster recovery means redeploying and issuing new tokens: the stack files hold the whole desired state, and the tokens are the only secrets.
Create a new Swarm on a new manager and join the nodes (Create the swarm). Label the proxy node again. Create a new token for each class, delete the old ones, and create the secrets (Rotate a runner token). Also create runner-placeholder-token, which every runner reads in place of a token, or the deploy fails with secret not found. On Linux: printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder. On Windows, use the placeholder step of windows/Setup.ps1 (The token proxy). Deploy the same stack files with your deploy variables, -c files and pins. Volumes are not recovered: the proxy starts with no state and asks CircleCI, and a persistent class starts with an empty volume. Restore the backup only to keep the node membership, or after a loss of quorum: stop Docker on the target manager, replace /var/lib/docker/swarm with the backup, start Docker, and run docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr . This makes a one-manager cluster with the old state. Unlock it if needed, check docker node ls and docker service ls, add managers and workers again, and back up again.
data.capacity-and-concurrency#Capacity and co:
The replicas of a class are the jobs it runs at once. A job with parallelism: n needs n replicas. To add replicas:
Check demand. unclaimed_task_count above 0 for several minutes with every replica busy means the class is full. The API needs a personal API token (runner API reference):
RUNNER_API=https://runner.circleci.com CLASS=/linux-default curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=$CLASS" Scale, then set the same replicas in your stack file:
docker service scale runners_linux-default= Check that the new replicas run. If they stay Pending, the node lacks CPU or memory for the reservations (Size the limits):
docker service ps runners_linux-default --filter desired-state=running Two limits sit above the replicas, both on the CircleCI side: the runner concurrency of your plan (shared by all self-hosted runner jobs of the organization) and maxConcurrentTasks of the resource class (20 by default, raised by CircleCI support). Queued tasks count against concurrency, and the inventory shows running tasks only, so runners can look idle while jobs wait. A job for a class with no runner queues indefinitely and holds concurrency: cancel it (Jobs wait while the runners are idle).
The stack has no autoscaling and no cloud integration, and a dead node is not replaced. Plan for one node less than you have. A labeled node of the token proxy carries no replicas (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves).
One token-proxy replica serves all classes of an OS, because a second would not share the list of runners that have claimed.
Limits: 0.5 CPU and 128 MB on Linux, 1 CPU and 512 MB on Windows. Load: 100 idle runners make 20 claims a second, plus the calls of running jobs. No fleet size is load-tested (CI runs a few replicas). Before more than a few dozen replicas, test with your load. Watch docker stats --no-stream on its node, 503 answers with Retry-After in runner logs, and the claim count in its summary line. If the proxy is the bottleneck, raise its limits in your copy of the stack file. A second stack (own name, proxy, classes and tokens) is untested.
data.check-status-and-logs#Check status and l:
List services, replicas and tasks (finished tasks stay for a short time, and the ERROR column says why a task failed or stays pending):
docker stack services runners docker stack ps runners --no-trunc Read a class. On Linux, entrypoint lines start with circleci-runner-entrypoint::
docker service logs --tail 100 --follow runners_linux-default On Linux, read the distributor. Its runner-distributor: lines say which version the node installs and when the link current moves:
docker service logs --tail 50 runners_runner-distributor In the web app, Runners lists the replicas of each class. A name you do not recognize means someone else holds a token of that class. Healthy single-task replicas show a steady stream of tasks ending in Complete, because every finished job ends a task. Alert on:
Tasks that end with a non-zero exit code, including 80 and 1. Exit code 143 needs no action: a replica that gets SIGTERM while it still retries to reach CircleCI at start-up exits with 143. Log lines that start with circleci-runner: error or circleci-runner-entrypoint: error, and lines with 401. In the distributor log: cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, error. Tasks that stay Pending. Many tasks of one node that end within seconds: a node can stay Ready and fail every job it claims (Many jobs fail within seconds on one node).
data.circleci-server-proxies-and-hosts-withou:
Two setups are not tested yet: CircleCI server, and an installation with no route to the internet. Nothing here promises either works.
CircleCI server. The proxy takes the runner API address in its -upstream argument, in the command of token-proxy in the stack file. The CI runs against CircleCI cloud and a fake API, never a server installation. Open questions: whether the claim and scale calls match your server version, which runner versions your server accepts (the default pin is tested against cloud only), and whether the proxy and runner trust your server’s certificate (the table below). Run the canary first, and do not assume anything on this page was checked for your version. An air-gapped installation. It does not work with this release: every runner container downloads its task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com at start, and no setting redirects that. Nodes must reach that host, directly or through a proxy the runner honors.
data.compatibility-with-circleci#Compatibilit:
The token proxy sits between the runner and CircleCI, so it depends on the runner API more closely than a plain runner install.
The proxy changes one call, POST /api/v3/runner/claim: a 2xx other than 204 means that CircleCI handed over a task, and the proxy latches that runner. At a start with no state it also reads GET /api/v3/runner/scale (data.attributes.running_task_count and unclaimed_task_count, whole numbers of 0 or more). Every other call is forwarded unchanged. Neither call is in CircleCI’s public runner API reference, and CircleCI does not promise that they stay as they are.
data.drain-a-node-for-patching#Drain a node f:
Restarting the Docker daemon stops every container (live restore does not work in Swarm mode), so empty the node before you patch Docker or reboot. On Linux, a drain sends SIGTERM and waits for the grace period, so running jobs finish. On Windows, use A Windows node instead.
Drain:
docker node update --availability drain Wait until no task runs on it. Swarm starts replacements elsewhere at once. If the other nodes lack capacity, they stay Pending until the drained tasks exit:
docker node ps Patch and reboot. Unlock a manager that uses autolock (Unlock a locked swarm).
Return the node to service:
docker node update --availability active Tasks do not move back by themselves, but single-task replicas restart after every job, so new tasks spread out again soon. Patch managers one at a time to keep the quorum (Managers and quorum), and the proxy node last (The node of the proxy).
data.free-disk-space#Free disk space: A full disk is the most common way a node stops running jobs, and a full manager disk can break Swarm itself.
data.if-a-token-leaked#If a token leaked:
The old token stays valid for anyone who holds it until it is deleted in CircleCI, so delete it before the swap. Delete it as soon as its replacement exists.
Create the new token and secret (steps 1 and 2 above). Delete the old token at once (the commands of step 6). CircleCI stops accepting it for new claims, and running jobs continue. A proxy or persistent runner that still holds the old secret fails with 401, so the class claims no new jobs until step 3 completes. Swap the secret as in step 3. Then replace the idle runners of a single-task class (docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_; on Windows, Replace refused runners on Windows). In a persistent class, add --update-parallelism 0 to the swap command so that every replica is replaced at once, each after its running job (on Windows, a running job ends: rerun it). Do steps 4 and 5, and remove the old secret. Then look for what the token did: unknown names in the runner inventory in CircleCI, and the jobs that ran on the class. A leaked single-task token did not come from a job in a runner container, because those hold no token. Look at who can read Swarm secrets (the docker group on a manager), at the proxy node, and at manager backups. Rotate the tokens of every class whose secret that path reached, because the proxy holds all of them.
data.keep-the-deploy-variables-in-version-con:
The variables of docker stack deploy are the only record of your choices that the stack files do not hold: the runner pin and its SHA-256 values, the proxy image, and the proxy placement. A deploy that leaves them out silently sets the defaults again: the shipped pin, the proxy tag latest, and the placement node.role == manager (which can move the proxy to a node without its state). A docker service update change is lost the same way.
Keep the variables in a file in your own repository next to your stack files, and never deploy by hand. deploy/deploy.env (no secrets):
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.13 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256= MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy@sha256: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' deploy/deploy.sh, the only way to deploy on Linux (add the -c files of your add-on stack files to the last line):
#!/bin/sh set -eu cd "$(dirname "$0")" set -a . ./deploy.env set +a exec docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml runners Run it with sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh: the script reads the file itself, so sudo need not keep the environment. Before the first deploy and after every edit, check that the values reach the stack. linux/setup.sh --deploy also warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.
(set -a; . deploy/deploy.env; set +a; docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml) | grep -E 'machine-runner-swarm.proxy ==|image: ccilabs' On Windows, load the file into the session and deploy from it:
Get-Content deploy\deploy.env | ForEach-Object { if ($_ -match '^\s*([^#=\s]+)\s*=\s*(.*)$') { Set-Item -Path "env:$($Matches[1])" -Value $Matches[2].Trim("'") } } docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners
data.monitor-the-cluster#Monitor the cluster:
On a manager:
docker service ls docker node ls docker stack ps runners --filter desired-state=running --format '{{.Name}} {{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -v Running This counts, per node, the tasks that ended within the last minute or so. A node with many such tasks either fails its jobs or has more work than the others (Many jobs fail within seconds on one node):
docker stack ps runners --format '{{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -E ' (Complete|Failed) [0-9]+ seconds? ago' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn The runner API shows what CircleCI sees (personal API token; runner.circleci.com on cloud, or your server’s runner API URL: CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet). Set RUNNER_API and CLASS as in Capacity and concurrency, then:
curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner?resource-class=$CLASS" | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.name) \(.last_connected)"' curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=$CLASS" Signal Where Alert when Replicas and nodes docker service ls, docker node ls Fewer replicas than desired for over 10 minutes (A task stays pending), a node not Ready, a manager Unreachable, or no Leader Runners connected /api/v3/runner: items, last_connected Fewer items than replicas, or last_connected older than 2 minutes Jobs that wait or run /api/v3/runner/tasks: unclaimed_task_count. /api/v3/runner/tasks/running: running_runner_tasks unclaimed_task_count above 0 for several minutes (concurrency). running_runner_tasks equal to the replicas for a long time: the class is full Task exits, distributor docker service ps, docker service ps runners_runner-distributor Exit code 80, a restart loop (The container restarts every 10 seconds), fewer distributor tasks than Linux nodes, cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, or not adopting it (current is not a version the distributor follows) Disk df -h /var/lib/docker on every node, docker system df Above 80 percent on a worker, 70 percent on a manager (Free disk space) Token proxy docker service ps runners_token-proxy, docker stats --no-stream on its node, its summary line Restarts, CPU near the limit, or rising refused claims (Monitor the token proxy) A job that starts A canary job per class The canary fails, or does not start within a few minutes A canary job runs the whole path (web app, CircleCI, proxy, node, runner), so it catches what the Swarm view does not: a healthy proxy that refuses every runner, a class whose token CircleCI rejects, and a plan with no concurrency left. It does not say which node is at fault. Run it on a schedule from a project of your own, per class:
version: 2.1 jobs: canary: machine: true resource_class: /linux-default steps: - run: echo ok workflows: canary: when: equal: [scheduled_pipeline, << pipeline.trigger_source >>] jobs: - canary
data.monitor-the-token-proxy#Monitor the toke:
Every claim of a single-task class goes through the service token-proxy (Windows: token-proxy-windows, same log lines). It runs as one replica, and runners cannot claim without it (The token proxy).
docker service ps runners_token-proxy docker service logs --tail 30 runners_token-proxy GET /healthz answers 200 when every class has a usable token file. The health check is the proxy binary with -healthcheck (/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Linux, C:\machine-runner-swarm-proxy.exe on Windows), because the images have no curl or wget. Swarm runs it every 10 seconds and restarts the task after 3 failures. A start can take up to 25 seconds before the proxy listens, so start_period is 30 seconds on Linux and 40 on Windows. The log has one line per event and never a token:
Log line Meaning listening on :8080, upstream , classes tasks.linux-default,... Started. One class per secret -token it holds. A class missing here gets 403 from its runners: its secret is not mounted in token-proxy or not named -token claim from (tasks.): upstream status 204 or 200 204: no task (normal, about every 5 seconds per idle runner). 200: a task was handed out, and that runner cannot claim again released (tasks.) DNS has not listed the address for 30 seconds in a row: the container is gone, and a new one on that address may claim claim from refused: not a runner of any class (tasks. lists [...], ...) Not a runner of a configured class, or one DNS does not list yet. Compare with the addresses in the line. Look for a class added without adding it to the proxy claim from refused: this runner has already claimed a task A second claim from one container. After a restart, a runner that has claimed gets this until Swarm replaces it (Restart the proxy) claim from refused: too many claims More than 2 claims a second from one container (429) state: cannot write it: ... When the proxy cannot save its state claim from (tasks.): upstream status 401 CircleCI rejects the class token: deleted, or the secret holds another class’s token (The runner log shows 401) upstream error: ... The proxy node cannot reach the runner API, or the connection broke (runners get 502). A claim that had reached CircleCI is latched (A claim whose outcome is unknown) cannot resolve the runners, token file Swarm DNS or a class secret is unavailable (runners get 503). No latch is released meanwhile One summary line a minute Claims forwarded, latched and refused, refusals by reason. Rising refusals while runners are healthy point to the causes above. The wording can change between releases: alert on the numbers Limits. Each client IP gets 2 claims a second (burst 10, answer 429) and 50 requests a second (burst 200) on all paths. At most 512 requests are served at once, and one above that gets 503 with Retry-After. The proxy waits 60 seconds for CircleCI’s response headers. A runner and a job stay far below these numbers.
If the proxy is down, runners cannot claim and CircleCI keeps jobs queued. A runner that runs a job keeps its container, but its calls to the API wait. linux/tests/proxy.sh measures this with the real runner: a restart while jobs run does not end them, and a proxy that is down when jobs end only delays the report. Swarm restarts a failed proxy task after 5 seconds on Linux and 10 on Windows. Do not leave the proxy down long while jobs run: how long the task agent keeps retrying is not documented.
data.no-unattended-changes#No unattended chan:
An update that restarts the Docker daemon or the node ends every container on it (on Windows that kills jobs). On every node, switch off whatever patches or restarts without you:
Windows. Set the Windows Update policy to download and notify. Install and reboot only in the procedure above. Debian and Ubuntu. Set Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "false". Hold the Docker packages, because a docker-ce upgrade restarts the daemon: sudo apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io (and unhold for the planned upgrade). Set needrestart to list only: $nrconf{restart} = 'l';. RHEL and its clones. Turn off automatic installation in dnf-automatic (or limit it to a download), and version-lock the Docker packages.
data.node-death#Node death:
Swarm marks a node Down after it misses its heartbeats and starts replacement tasks on other nodes that match the constraints.
The jobs on the node are lost. CircleCI reports them as failed because of a problem with your infrastructure. Self-hosted runners have no automatic retry: rerun the workflow from the failed job. Services pinned to the node stay Pending: the persistent class (node.hostname) and the docker-build classes (a labeled node). Capacity drops by the node’s replicas until it returns or other nodes have room. A returning node rejoins by itself while its certificate is valid. Swarm does not move tasks back. A node gone for good: docker node rm --force . For a lost manager use docker node demote (if reachable) or docker node rm --force, and add a new manager to hold the quorum. The cluster runs while a majority of managers remains. Without one, running jobs finish but no replica is replaced (Managers and quorum).
data.optional-an-image-that-lets-a-job-finish:
Your own image can lift the limit by setting WaitToKillServiceTimeout once, at build time, in milliseconds: at least your longest job plus a margin. This example is 18,300,000 (5 hours and 5 minutes, the max_run_time of the runner plus 5 minutes):
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 RUN reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control /v WaitToKillServiceTimeout /t REG_SZ /d 18300000 /f Set the value at build time: Windows reads it only when the container boots, so reg add in a running container does nothing. Use the image as the image: of the service, which still mounts the runner and Git and sets PATH as in the shipped stack file. Build one image per Server Core tag, and rebuild it after each Patch Tuesday update of the base image.
Warning Never use New-Item -Force on an existing registry key, in an image build or a running container. It deletes the values and subkeys of the key, and on the cexecsvc service key the container then fails to start with hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded. Use reg add or Set-ItemProperty.
Machine runner swarm does not build or test such an image. Before you rely on it, run a job of a few minutes on a non-production node, force an update of its service, and check that the job finishes.
data.pin-a-version#Pin a version:
The default is an exact pin. Pin when a runner change must go through your change process, then upgrade by changing the pin or taking a newer release. The default SHA-256 list belongs to the default pin, so a pin of your own needs its values in the same command, from the checksums.txt of that runner release, for every architecture of your nodes:
sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.12 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=, docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Put the same two values in deploy/deploy.env. The distributor installs only a tarball with one of these values. Without the list it refuses the tarball (SHA-256 mismatch) and the nodes keep the running version. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest trusts the manifest instead (weaker). If you edit the pin in your copy of the stack file, change both defaults together in x-distributor-env (and in x-env of microvm.yaml, which downloads the runner itself). Use 3.1.12 or later: it fixes the enforcement of max_run_time.
Freeze the nodes now. Pin the version the nodes run now (See what runs). It is installed, so no network is needed. Record the same two values in deploy/deploy.env:
docker service update --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION= --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest runners_runner-distributor
data.prevent-it#Prevent it:
Set the task history limit. docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 keeps at most 2 finished tasks per slot. The single-node setup of linux/setup.sh sets it. A swarm you create yourself does not (Create the swarm).
Give Docker its own filesystem, and keep managers free of jobs. Put /var/lib/docker on a separate volume, sized for the worst case above: replicas, times the largest workspace, times (1 plus the history limit), plus images. A manager with the proxy label runs no jobs.
Prune images on every node, on a schedule. Swarm has no command that runs on every node, and a global service with the Docker socket would be root everywhere, so use each node’s scheduler (configuration management, or a systemd timer on Linux). Install the two units of examples/systemd in /etc/systemd/system. The service removes images no container uses that are older than a week, and the timer runs it every Sunday:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now docker-image-prune.timer until filters by image creation time, not last use, and --all skips every image a container (stopped ones too) still uses. A removed image that is needed again is pulled again, so a mirror (What needs internet) must be up. On a docker-build node, add docker builder prune --force --filter until=168h. On Windows, run the same docker image prune from a scheduled task. The Server Core and distributor images are in use while the stack runs, so a prune keeps them.
Alert on every node’s disk (df -h /var/lib/docker): above 80 percent on a worker, 70 percent on a manager (Monitor the cluster).
Warning Do not run docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes on a node of this stack. The named volumes hold runner-bin, proxy-state and the persistent classes. A volume no container uses at that moment (for example a persistent class scaled to 0) is deleted with its data. Leave docker container prune to the task history too, except in an emergency.
data.proxies-and-certificate-authorities-comp:
Each component has its own network stack, so a variable that works for one does nothing for another. Only the Linux distributor row was tested, with BusyBox 1.37.0 of alpine:3 against a stub proxy, not a real corporate proxy. The other rows follow from how each program is written, and the CI does not test them.

data.recycle-a-class#Recycle a class:
A forced update replaces every replica of a service one at a time, each with a runner drain. Use it to move a persistent class to a new runner version, or to reset it. On Windows, recycle a class only while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).
docker service update --force runners_linux-persistent Recycling removes only the container filesystem. The named volume survives, so /home/circleci (Linux) and C:\cache (Windows) keep their files. To reset the volume too, scale the service to 0, run docker volume rm runners_persistent-home (Linux) or docker volume rm runners_windows-persistent-cache (Windows) on the node that holds it, and scale back up.
On Linux, a persistent class does not clean its working directory: the runner user cannot remove files the job user owns, so the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". Start every job on that class with a step that removes what an earlier job left, and recycle the class on a schedule (Working directory cleanup).
data.replace-refused-runners-on-windows#Repla:
docker service update --force replaces every container of a service at once, busy ones included, so on a Windows class it ends running jobs. A refused runner (403 this runner has already claimed a task) holds no task, so removing that one container is safe, and Swarm starts a replacement. The CI does not run these commands: check the result before you use them on a fleet.
On a manager, list the addresses the proxy refused in the last minutes:
docker service logs --since 5m runners_token-proxy-windows 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" } | Select-String 'claim from (\S+) refused: this runner has already claimed a task' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Sort-Object -Unique On each Windows node, list the class’s containers with their addresses and find those from step 1:
docker ps -q --filter 'name=runners_windows-default' | ForEach-Object { docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}} {{end}}' $_ } Remove only those, by name:
docker rm -f <CONTAINER_NAME> Or wait: a refused runner recycles at its idle timeout (1 hour). Do not shorten the timeout now: a stack file change is a service update and stops the busy containers too.
data.restart-the-proxy#Restart the proxy:
A restart is safe at any time, on the same node. The proxy keeps the addresses of runners that have claimed in the volume proxy-state and refuses only those afterwards. A runner that has not claimed may claim, so no restart, deploy or reboot locks a runner out.
Restart (Windows: runners_token-proxy-windows):
docker service update --force runners_token-proxy Read the start line:
